speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of State and Minister of State (Treasury Board)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board)
subsubtopic: ALLEGED COERCION TO FALSIFY TRAVEL CLAIMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. In an article in The Ottawa Citizen dated Tuesday, September 20, 1988, an ex-employee, Grace McCaffrey, alleges that she was coerced into falsifying travel claims.
Miss McCaffrey became seriously ill shortly after she became a permanent employee of my office. We held the job open for her while she recovered her health. Two months later she resigned.
Miss McCaffrey makes no direct charge as to who coerced or encouraged her to fabricate the "reason for travel". At no time during her employment in my office did she raise this issue with myself or Miss Janet Binks, my executive assistant. We are surprised that she would wait six months to raise such a serious charge.
I have asked my staff if there is any truth to this allegation. They have assured me that they have no knowledge of any threat, coercion, or encouragement in connection with travel claims, or any other matter. To the best of our knowledge, all travel claims before, during and after Miss McCaffrey's employment have been completed in accordance with the regulations. There is absolutely no truth to these allegations.
[DOT] (mo)
However, I have asked the Privy Council Office to oversee an investigation into these allegations, and the PCO has arranged with the Comptroller General to conduct an audit of the travel claims submitted during Miss McCaffrey's term of employment to ensure that they are in compliance with the regulations for travel by Ministers and their staff. The results of this audit will be made public as soon as they are made available.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED COERCION TO FALSIFY TRAVEL CLAIMS

I take it that when the Minister makes public the results of the investigation we will have answers to those questions because I understand only a Minister can sign such claims.

Madam Speaker, let me just quickly go through my amendment, Motion No. 49, and make a couple of comments about the amendments moved by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). I keep telling this story, to the Hon. Member's consternation, but I want to warn him that there is an election coming. The House will recall Robert McGregor, who used to be the Member for York East for about 22 years. They called him Silent Bob McGregor because he did not speak for 22 years, then he made the mistake of getting up and moving a motion and was defeated in the next election.
One of our concerns in the NDP with Clause 5(2) as it stands is that it does not clearly indicate that the system should facilitate Canadian programming in particular. It must be made patently clear, we believe, to the CRTC, the regulatory body, that it should give priority to Canadian programming services over others. This has already been stated in Clause 3(1 )(r) and should be reiterated here. I find it difficult to understand how the Minister can oppose this motion which I think is consistent with past reports and the history of broadcasting policy in Canada.
I want to make a few comments about Motions Nos. 56, 67 and 68 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for York East. I have no objection to Motion No. 56 which involves protection of non-English or French services in case of difficulties with the carriage arrangements with cable companies. It gives priority to program undertakings in such disputes. It was submitted, I believe, by the Ethnocultural Council and I could support that.
Motion No. 67 would permit a new public hearing on matters referred back to the CRTC by the Cabinet through its power of review. As the amendment explains, this is not a bad idea as it will permit the public to express itself at such hearings and perhaps open up the process a bit. That is supportable.
Motion No. 68 is where the Hon. Member's streak ends, as far as I am concerned. I find this an extraordinary amendment, perhaps because it is from an extraordinary Member. It says that any order or regulation made by the CRTC under Section 9 or Section 10 would be laid before Parliament for 30
September 20, 1988

days before it comes into effect. At least 15 MPs or 8 Senators, if they filed a motion that the proposed order or regulation not be put in place, could cause a vote on that motion. If the MPs win the vote, the CRTC regulation or order could not be carried out.
To put it mildly, I find this a recipe for regulatory and parliamentary chaos. It is also a recipe for massive political interference in the affairs of the CRTC. This is a little bit of back-bench dinosaur type of thinking of the Conservative Party. Perhaps my friend will explain it as opening up the process for participatory democracy or something like that, but I would like him to deal with the fact that it seems to me it will mean chaos. The CRTC is a quasi-judicial body, and what does he want to do? He wants us to review the decisions of that body after we have given it the power to make certain decisions. He wants to drag some controversial matters back into Parliament after the CRTC has dealt with them. Perhaps the Hon. Member can explain himself.
However, I can support his other motions and I hope he will support my Motion No. 49, as I would think the Minister would support it. Once again, it deals with strengthening Canadian programming and giving choices to Canadians so they can see good quality Canadian programming and we are not submerged in the North Americanization of the media that this Bill will bring in as well as the Government's free trade legislation.
Those are my amendments and my comments on the amendments of the Hon. Member for York East.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to these three amendments that I have laid before the House, which deal with three different issues. I am not entirely sure why it was decided that they were to be grouped for debate, but let me say I want to deal very briefly with the first one, Motion No. 56, and then spend most of my time with Motion No. 68.
Motion No. 56, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has pointed out, was originally suggested before the legislative committee by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council. It was one of its submissions. I put it forward also in light of concerns that had been raised with me by my own constituents and by ethnic broadcasters in Metropolitan Toronto. One of the great concerns, particularly with broadcasters who are involved with a closed-circuit FM broadcasting from cable television is that their existence, their career and livelihood are dependent upon the whims of cable companies. They can be cut off at a moment's notice. I refer specifically to Mr. Gus Agathos who broadcasts in this fashion in Metropolitan Toronto. He is a Greek broadcaster who has been on the air for years and years but is constantly under the threat of being cut off by the Rogers Cable Company. There is the possibility that all of his lifetime of work, the business he has built up with his listeners, can just be wiped out by some sort of arbitrary decision without some form of appeal. This
Broadcasting Act
motion would give at least some form of mediation to that process.
A second problem Mr. Agathos and others like him have is the lack of access to other cable companies within the Metropolitan Toronto area. Because of the monopolistic distribution of cable franchises, one part of Metropolitan Toronto has one cable company, another part has another cable company and still another part has another cable company. He can only broadcast by negotiating with one cable company. While his potential audience lives all over Metropolitan Toronto and beyond, he is limited by the geographic territorial limits of the cable company's franchise. This would hopefully give Mr. Agathos and people like him some opportunity to deal with the CRTC and the cable companies in a way that would give him at least a little more right than he has now.
Moving on to Motion No. 67, this is aimed at allowing for public participation in the process. Again this is a suggestion put forward by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council to the legislative committee, and one which I as a great supporter of the principle of democracy and public input wholeheartedly endorse.
Motion No. 68, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) pointed out, is somewhat unique, but not entirely unique in the annals of Parliament. If the Hon. Member had carefully been following what has been happening in this Parliament he would know that in Bill C-72, in amendments to the bilingual legislation, a provision of this kind was incorporated in the Bill as passed by Parliament. It was a provision agreed to by the Government in that piece of legislation and it is part of the law of Canada at the present time. 1 suggest that we incorporate a similar provision in this legislation.
I again go back to my concern relating to condominium owners. Here where a regulation comes down we have been assured by the Minister there will be exemption for condominiums broadcasting with satellite systems, but the Minister may not be around forever, as suggested by some. We would like to see her around forever but immortality has so far escaped the human soul.
Oh, oh!

As a result of that, with another Minister, with another CRTC, even with the same CRTC, who knows what it may do with respect to the rights of condominium broadcasters with satellite systems? If the CRTC should by any chance bring down a regulation which would include a condominium satellite TV system as a cable company, this would give Parliament the right to deal with that sort of regulation and reject it. This would be protection for what the Minister is telling us will come to pass and will give Parliament that right as far as condominium ownership is concerned.
That raises the whole issue of the concerns of condominium owners. I agree with them that this legislation is discriminatory against them with respect to their position vis-a-vis a single

September 20, 1988
Broadcasting Act
family detached dwelling owner. As far as condominium owners are concerned, if they are to be regulated as a cable company, that leaves them with no alternative reception, whereas a single family homeowner would have an alternative. If that single family homeowner did not want a cable company, the individual could always put a satellite receiver in his or her backyard and not be regulated. That is not the case under this legislation as far as a condominium owner is concerned. Condominium owners stand to be regulated under the legislation as it is now, apart from the assurances of the Minister, as if they were a cable company. There is no alternative to opting, as a single family home owner can.
In fact, as you know, Madam Speaker, systems that condominium corporations operate as far as satellite television reception are concerned are operated on a non-profit basis. They are not a commercial undertaking. They are operated basically by volunteers. If they are to be regulated, most of these volunteers have told me, and I am sure this will happen, they will just throw up their hands and walk away from the systems, leaving condominium owners no other alternative but to fall into the clutches, if you will, of a cable company. The cable company then will be the only one that can offer them television reception service.
The whole thrust of this motion is to protect condominium owners, to give Parliament the right to deal with that, and to make sure that what we are being told is that condominium systems will not be regulated.
The legislation as it now stands, we have been told in response to my specific questions at the legislative committee, not only will catch condominium satellite television systems but also satellite television systems that may be in a senior citizens' home. Senior citizens' homes in my riding such as True Davidson Acres, the Mennonite Home, the Canadian Macedonia Place and the Ina Grafton Gage Home stand to be caught and regulated by this legislation unlike a single family dwelling which will not be.
For all of these reasons it seems to me essential that if the Minister somehow or other leaves this post thousands of years down the line and we have another Minister, or if the CRTC changes its stripe or philosophy and suddenly comes up with a regulation that does catch condominiums and senior citizens' homes, under Motion No. 68 that regulation would come here to this House and if 15 Members of Parliament thought that was objectionable-surely there would be at least that number-we would then have an opportunity to deal with it. If we felt that it was improper to regulate condominium satellite television systems and systems going into poor, benighted senior citizens' homes, then we could deal with it here and reject it.
It is on that basis that I put forward this motion and I commend it to the Minister and the Government. I hope she
and the Government will see fit to adopt not only Motion No. 68 but Motions Nos. 56 and 67 as well.

Madam Speaker, Motion No. 56 relates to Clause 10 and indicates the Hon. Member's desire to have protection of distribution undertakings in order to protect the financial viability of programming undertakings or to ensure the retransmission by distribution undertakings of programs produced in a language other than English or French. Certainly if these programs have been licensed by the CRTC and have received the approval of those communities to which they relate, as is the case with TeleLatino or Chinavision, et cetera, I think this is a very worthwhile amendment. If it does that, I would certainly support it.
I would like to support the motion of my colleague from Vancouver-Kingsway as well. I think it too is a very worthwhile amendment. The Hon. Member is saying that the Canadian broadcasting system should be regulated and supervised in a flexible manner, and with that I am totally in accord, and that in and during that regulatory process by the CRTC, the provisions of Canadian programs to Canadians should be facilitated. I think that is the fundamental issue facing us as Canadians and as legislators here in the House of Commons.
It is with somewhat of a sense of sadness that I have been watching the whole process unravel. This is a very important Bill for Canadians and for Canadian content. It is so technical that very few people who are watching this debate sense the real vitality and importance of the thrust of this whole Bill. I had hoped that the thrust would be the Canadianization of the Canadian broadcasting system.
Although the Minister has brought some substantive measures forward, she has also done a fair degree of tinkering. I do not see this as being a partisan issue. I think this is a fundamental issue, irrespective of which Government is in place. We are talking about policies that will endure much longer than any Minister or any Government.
The system will not be Canadian in many ways. It will be a North American system. The Bill really provides for the continentalization of our system. The Minister knows fundamentally that we are not dealing with satellite-to-cable networks which can limit the additional American programs that will have access to our system. She has not accepted constructive amendments which would ensure predominantly Canadian content, nor has she ensured carriage priorities on our cable system in law, issues which will also affect the advertising income of our own broadcasters and will have an impact on the business community.
When I spoke to the Minister about the importance of the amendments brought forward in Motion No. 45 and Motion No. 37, I felt that she was ignoring the fundamental direction of this whole Bill which is that it is a Canadian Bill. Broadcasters cannot even be assured of the exclusivity of Canadian rights. American majors, as she knows, including ABC, NBC
September 20, 1988

and CBS, are players in the field. They can bring programs into our market which carry non-simultaneous advertising because they are in a different time period.
I tried, through amendments, to grandfather every network that we already have in the system, the 17 that were there previously and the five new ones, the 22 stations. My motion provided that we could bring in other American programs as long as they are complementary services, not competitive services. I think I have made it very clear that my intention is not to block out what is new, exciting and dynamic but it is to ensure a Canadian broadcasting system. This, regretfully, the Minister has not seen fit to accept.
I talked about the importance of limiting foreign programming carriage, services that would change substantially what we have now, but complementary services are totally acceptable. In the opening clause of 3(l)(a), we say that the first obligation of the Canadian broadcasting system is to provide a public service essential to the maintenance and enhancement of national identity and cultural sovereignty.
I would suggest that the mechanisms for which we have asked have not been dealt with. Perhaps if we accept the amendment proposed to the CRTC's mandate that would provide that it knows what the Minister and the Government want, that they want a Canadian broadcasting system with Canadian programming, it may well facilitate that.
I sincerely hope that my sense of sadness will be alleviated by some changes that will be accepted by the Minister so we can see in the long run networks that are direct broadcast services and so we can see a diminishing access by new American services in the light in which I think many Canadians see it. They have access to American programming in many ways, and I think that enough is enough. Now let us promote Canadians and let the broadcasters find the financing mechanisms that they need. They need advertising revenue. They cannot sell their stuff if they cannot advertise because their audience is disappearing.
I would suggest to the Minister that she find some more constructive mechanisms, as she has tried to do to date, so that we can have the kind of Canadian broadcasting system that we want.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the discussion on this motion. We are attempting to provide more Canadian programming for more Canadians and I do not expect that there would be a single Member of the House of Commons who would not support that principle. 1 do not think there would be a single Canadian who would not like to see more Canadian programming on television.
To make this case very clear, it is my privilege to present the following motion. I move: "That Motion No. 49 be amended to read as follows: That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 5 by adding after line 33 on page 8 the following: Subsection (e), facilitates the provision of Canadian programs to Canadians."

speechtext: After reading the amendment to the motion which the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap has presented, the Chair will want to reserve, because at first reading, it seems that the Hon. Member may want to amend the Bill further and not actually the motion which is before the House. I will reserve on the motion and will study it further.

Madam Speaker, I realize that you have reserved on this, but I think it is important to point out that what the original Motion No. 49 did, which the Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) put forward and which the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) automatically adopted, not understanding what it would do to broadcasting in Canada. Unfortunately, it would have had the impact of reducing the extension of services of all broadcasting to those communities, those isolated areas, to which we are trying to direct the extension of services for all broadcasting. We intend to carry that out. We do not want to limit the extension of service.
What the proposed amendment to the amendment is seeking to undertake is to extend as well Canadian programming. It has been stated many times before in this Bill, and I have no difficulty in stating it again. It is somewhat redundant. It is the provision of Canadian programs to Canadians, but it must not interfere with the extension of all services across Canada to people who are not now able to receive them.
I would say, in looking at the proposal, even though you have not ruled on it as yet, that it does have my acquiescence.
With regard to the other matters, I would just say briefly to the Member for York East (Mr. Redway) that I want to assure him, with regard to his Amendment No. 56, that the Bill does cover all languages and not just English and French. Any kind of broadcasting that is done in other languages has to come under the rubric of the Broadcasting Act, and we have taken measures throughout to ensure that that will be both honoured and acknowledged. There is no question of trying to retain broadcasting only in the two official languages. As you know, we have many stations that do broadcast and program in other languages.
With regard to Motion No. 67, regarding hearings in relation to the CBC, the CRTC always holds public hearings in relation to the renewal of or the application for licences by the CBC. That is automatically done, and I want to leave it up to the CRTC to follow that practice, and not say that you must do this with one hearing and you must do that with another.
There is a final amendment that I would like to speak to. I have tried to direct my concern to the problems that the Member for York East sees with regard to condominiums. I am very conscious of it and I know that in the past, in the 1968 Bill, regulations did apply to cable, condominiums, and multiunit dwellings. Exceptions were granted by the CRTC at that

September 20, 1988
Broadcasting Act
time. I have said many times that I expect that to continue. There is no reason to believe that it will not continue.
While I understand the goal of this particular amendment, to try to get even greater certainty for that particular group of people, nevertheless the proposal here would be so onerous, both on Parliament and on people who are involved in the broadcasting industry, waiting for decisions, that I think it would in effect be somewhat of an overkill.
The CRTC in fact issues hundreds of regulations and decisions on issues all the time. To have all these coming before Parliament might very well block everything else that Parliament is able to accomplish. We do not get through very much here as it is.
I want to assure him once again that I have his concerns in mind. I will continue to stress them and I will make a point of conveying that to the CRTC.

She said: Madam Speaker, Motions Nos. 53 and 54 go together. Motions Nos. 59, 60, and 69 are consequential amendments to Motion No. 58. Motions Nos. 53 and 54 deal with a procedural matter which is far more procedural than it would seem on the surface. This motion would delete the words "either in the form proposed or revised in such manner as the Governor in Council deems advisable".
The present wording would allow the Cabinet to alter directions to the CRTC that may be fundamentally different from what was originally laid before the Houses of Parliament. This would result in no opportunity for public hearings on the revised direction. We have said time and time again that in the field of broadcasting there is to be no Governor in Council intervention. It is to be an open process and what takes place must be known by the general public.

September 20, 1988
Broadcasting Act
The purpose of the motion is to remove the possibility of unwarranted pressures on a Minister and interference in the very sensitive broadcasting area. If anyone should know about the sensitivity of broadcasting and the impact it has on the country it is Members of Parliament whose interpretations are out there for the public to see and who count on the broadcasting media to get their message out.
Whatever the issue-today the truckers, yesterday free trade, tomorrow the taxation Bill-this is a very sensitive industry and it must be treated by Government in the most arm's length fashion in order that we cannot be perceived to be interfering. Unfortunately we are now getting to the point again where the length of one's arm is to the shoulder, and I do not think that that ensures an open process.
I recognize that the Bill cannot direct a House committee on how it should deal with proposed broad policy directions. One can hope it would deal with it, or even expect that it would deal with it, but we cannot direct it to deal with it.
The standing committee made it very clear, first, that it felt that broad policy directives should be tied directly to broadcasting policy as outlined in Clause 3, which the Government has not done directly and, second, that the broad policy directive be heard. Therefore I have proposed in Motion No. 54 that we agree to a process of developing a broad public direction which should be held and involved in a public hearing.
So Bill C-136, while containing provisions for referring directions to committees, is unable to require that a committee hold such hearings. It is for this reason that I bring this amendment forward. I hope that the Minister will be receptive of this amendment because it is asking the commission, in the case of the absence of action on a broad policy directive by the House, or by either part of the House, to hold such a hearing. I believe that this would open up the process.
In Motion No. 54 I have recommended the addition of Clause 5 which would state:
The Commission shall hold a public hearing, unless such committee of either House of Parliament has held public hearings pursuant to subsection 8(2), in connection with a proposed order by the Governor in Council, after the order is published in the Canada Gazette in accordance with subsection 8(1), or unless the Commission is satisfied that such a hearing is not in the public interest.
I think that leaves the commission, the Minister, the Governor in Council, and everyone else with enough latitude.
I would like to deal with the last of the series of my amendments in this particular block of motions. Here I am addressing fundamental and basic procedural fairness in the rule of law. I suggest, through you, Madam Speaker, to the Minister that through Clause 12 we have made the makers of rules, regulations, and orders judges in their own case. This is totally out of Canadian and democratic concepts of fairness in law.
I am sure the Minister received, as did I, a brief from the Canadian Bar Association. They make the observation that Bill C-136 substantially increases the powers of the CRTC
over the broadcasting industry. They point out that any person involved in the broadcasting industry may be subjected to several different sanctions for failing to comply with a regulation, license condition, decision, or order of the CRTC. In creating duplicate offences and multiple sanctions, in their view, the Act places licensees in double jeopardy without sufficient protection. The problem is compounded by the fact that a licensee may be subjected to different orders or decisions issued by one or more panels of the CRTC or even by the full commission itself.
The Minister knows there was a lot of discussion and that there is some disagreement and some serious concern about the use of panels on the "he who hears decides" concept. I think the Minister may be right, but we have to test that out. However, we certainly must be very careful about procedural fairness, and that is what the Canadian Bar Association is talking about.
Through the different powers granted to the CRTC by this Bill it becomes the lawmaker, the law interpreter, and the law enforcer at the same time. The Bar Association says that while this position is not uncommon in the administrative law field, it does give rise to concern that duplicate offences or penalties should be reduced to a minimum.
The purpose of my Motions Nos. 58, 59, 60 and 69, is that the courts would decide upon breaches of orders and regulations and the CRTC would decide upon breaches of conditions of licence. The reason I leave breaches of conditions of licences with the CRTC is that the conditions which we now put as a punishable offence on summary conviction are frequently very elaborate in detail and could easily be subject to a subjective interpretation.
1 believe the CBC supported me in this respect, that conditions are not solid grounds for prosecution in the criminal courts. Furthermore, since there are tailored conditions of licence by the commission, I think that is the best place to deal with it.
Therefore, I suggest that the Minister reconsider these particular clauses. She should review Clauses 12 and 13, then bring in the appropriate motions I have made and be supportive of the fact that we talked about fairness in rule of law.
You cannot be judged in your own case. That is not the Canadian way. I ask the Minister to give that very serious consideration.

Madam
Speaker, I can support Motions Nos. 53 and 54 brought forward by the Hon. Member because I believe they would lead to a more open public process. I believe that the Member has already cited the relevant testimony we received in committee from such groups as the Canadian Ethnocultural Council among others.
September 20, 1988

Motion No. 58 is more difficult. The CBC objected to this. I suppose it depends on one's assessment of what is an unreasonable power that the CRTC would have. I believe that it is not an unreasonable power. Accordingly, I would not support that motion.
Motion No. 59 simply adds the word "decision" to this section, meaning that the CRTC decisions as well as mandatory orders may be made orders of the Federal Court. Again, that sounds like a reasonable amendment.
Motion No. 69 deletes the clause that makes the breach of a licence condition. If you breach a licence condition set down by the regulatory body of the CRTC, you can be guilty of an offence punishable by summary conviction. The CBC and others feel that the conditions of a licence are by nature not grounds for prosecution in the criminal courts.
I took the opposite view in committee and said that, in fact, there are two different penalties set down in the Act. If you breach a regulation you get some sort of penalty. If you breach an order you get another sort of penalty. I thought that was inconsistent.
1 draw the Minister's attention to the hearings of the legislative committee as reported at page 10:143 to 10:146, where I deal with the Minister and Mr. Kinsman, her official, and some other people on this issue.
I oppose the amendment by the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), but I believe that there are some inconsistencies in the Bill as it is set out. 1 do not think it is a major matter, but there are inconsistencies. That is the position of our Party on this particular group of amendments.

Madam Speaker, with respect to policy directions to the CRTC it is important to recognize what is being proposed in this legislation in the way of hearings, consultations and so on.
The Minister must consult with the CRTC on a policy directive. Bringing in this new power of policy direction lays certain requirements on the Governor in Council and on the Minister. The Minister must consult with the CRTC about any policy directive. It is then published in the Canada Gazette with calls for comments. Third, it is tabled in the House of Commons and referred to committee for 40 days for consideration and response. Fourth, there is a second consultation with the CRTC. Finally, the CRTC can then decide whether or not to hold public hearings on general criteria and processes of implementation.
What we have is a very lengthy consultation process on any new policy directive. I think that indeed enhances the process and gives a great deal of latitude for public input and for parliamentary consideration.
With regard to mandatory orders, I think it is very important to recognize that this is indeed an important new power and something which I think will enhance the work of the CRTC. I know that the former Chairman of the CRTC felt,
Broadcasting Act
having worked with the existing powers either to revoke a licence or to administer a slap on the wrist to someone, that neither one was effective. This new power to issue mandatory orders is an important new power and one that I think should be welcomed.
Finally, I just want to say that on the question of legal remedies for a breach of condition of licence, there may well be some argument about this. I want it to be noted that the route we have taken in leaving it with the CRTC was a recommendation of Caplan-Sauvageau, who were in favour of this route, as was the standing committee.

Motion No. 57
That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 10 by striking out line 4 at page 13 and substituting the following therefor:
"of one or more classes, or to any persons or class of persons who are exempted from the requirement to hold a licence by subsection 9(2) or section 25."
Motion No. 61

"(d) the making of an order under subsection 9(2)".
She said: Madam Speaker, Motion No. 57 is an amendment to Clause 10(2), which in a sense I am hopeful will allow for a level playing field for all distribution systems and which looks at regulations for exempted persons.
Motion No. 61 will ensure public hearings if an exemption takes place. That is found in Clause 17.
Motion No. 57 enlarges the list of regulations that are possible by the CRTC under the general powers of the commission as set out on page 13 of the Bill. It would define and enlarge the places in which licences could be applicable, or
the classes of licence that could be applicable. It would be applicable to one or more classes, or to any persons or class of persons who are exempted from the requirement to hold a licence by subsection 9(2) or Section 25. In essence, what the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) has been talking about, in a sense, would make the process a little more open and a little more fair, I would hope.
The Canadian Bar Association addressed this issue in its brief to the legislative committee. It said, and I quote, "In order to have a level playing ground MATV systems should be governed by the same rules as those applicabale to cable television systems or other distribution systems. Under the proposed Act, these rules could be applied directly through regulations or licence conditions, or indirectly by the terms of exemption orders under Subclause 9(2)".
The purpose of my suggestion is so that where the MATV and the SMATV systems want to bring in and have Canadian content and follow the local rules they will also have the right to get pay-TV, and the kinds of things which they are having a great deal of difficulty doing.
There is one omission in the Act, I believe. It is the fact that the regulations enacted by the commission under Clause 10 of Bill C-136 cannot be made applicable to exempted persons. Clause 10(2) states that the regulations are only applicable to persons holding licences.
This is contrary to recommendation 14 of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, a recommendation which is contained in our sixth report. I would like to remind the Minister about what we had to say, as well as what First Choice, Canadian Communications Corporation, recommended in support of the type of amendment I have brought forward.
First, the standing committee said in recommendation 14 that the power to exempt undertakings from the requirement to obtain a licence should be subject to the right to impose terms and conditions, and regulations applicable to licensees should also be able to be applied to exempted persons. This would permit the CRTC, for example, while exempting MATV systems to require such systems to meet the same obligations or requirements related to the carriage of services, or any other matters as would apply to cable television systems or other comparable licensed undertakings. If they are using our airwaves, and we have said they are to be exempted, then let us find a way to make it a legal exemption.
As well, First Choice, Canadian Communications Corporation, said that there is one omission in the Act, that is, the regulations to be enacted by the commission under Clause 10. Clause 10(2) states that regulations can only be applied to persons holding licences. I bring that to the attention of the Minister.
To implement this I have presented Motion No. 61 to the Minister. I am not quite sure if the wording of it might well raise some concerns with respect to its being too broad a net. I

have made the recommendation that the making of an order under subsection 9(2) would allow for this exemption clause to be a more open situation. Maybe it should state "substantial order". Maybe it should read "significant order." Perhaps it needs some kind of refinement, although I personally feel that it is broad enough to allow for the kind of approach that I have been talking about.
With respect to Motion No. 61, the goal is that subsection 9(2) would allow the CRTC the discretion to exempt persons who carry on broadcasting undertakings of any class from licensing and regulations. This is an expansion of Section 17(l)(e) of the 1968 Broadcasting Act that only permitted exemptions of broadcasting receiving undertakings from licensing. This is a good power. It is a great power. But because of the broadness of this expanded power there needs to be a public process to provide fairness for all the players in the Canadian broadcasting system. They should really know why x, y and z were exempted. The Canadian Cable Television Association has said, "The unilateral power to exempt is a very powerful mechanism. The language of this section is very broad, offering no checks or balances on the exercise of power to exempt".
Since the goal of the broadcast policy is the degree of fairness for all players, the rules of the game should be clear, understood and well-defined, and they go through open public process, through the CRTC, through hearings or through procedures. 1 would like to recommend that the Minister give serious consideration to accepting the amendments which I have proposed under Motion No. 61,

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On debate the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the Minister accepting those amendments. That leaves Motion No. 54A and Motion No. 64. Motion 64 is the amendment of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone). It is identical to my Motion No. 65 which was ruled out of order, because it was identical. I would, of course, support Motion No. 64.
I want to speak on Motion 54A. This is a very important motion. It states:
That Bill C-136 be amended in Clause 9 by adding immediately after line 34 at page 11 the following:
"(i) determine whether the rates charged by distribution undertakings are at all times just and reasonable, and if they are not, may revise them accordingly."
This amendment reflects the belief of the NDP that cable companies should be regulated by rate of return legislation, and as a result the prices charged to ordinary Canadian subscribers should, like telephone rates, be more closely linked to profits. This has enormous implications, and is extremely important to the average Canadian. It is a necessary protection for consumers who increasingly, especially in urban areas, but also to a great extent in rural areas, view cable as an essential service. Everybody wants cable today.
This is a particularly important amendment at this time because many Canadians are now faced with very substantial increases in cable fees. In the lower mainland of British Columbia, where I am from, whether it is in Port Moody, Belcarra, Coquitlam, loco, Port Coquitlam, or Burnaby, those areas are served by Rogers Cablevision which has a territorial monopoly on cable services. That means that my constituents, if they are unhappy with Rogers' prices or services, cannot move to another company. There is only one cable company, and they are stuck with it. I might add that this is a very lucrative area for Rogers as 95 per cent of the households are cabled.
A great deal of concern has been expressed about that part of the recent price increase which is paid to subsidize the addition of four new services: YTV, Vision TV, Weather Now, and Much Music. They have been added to the basic services in my area of British Columbia. The Sports network will be added next year. There is a lot of controversy about who does and who does not want those services.
The Minister will say that this is a matter for the CRTC. I can hear her argument now. However, as the Minister knows, the Cabinet has power of review over the CRTC decisions. The Minister should know this, because it is part of the same decision that brought those services into the basic service. The CRTC gave the licence for an all-news network to the CBC. Of course, at that time that was not acceptable to this present Cabinet. This was the only part of the decision on which the Minister decided to intervene. The Minister did intervene in this matter because of the pressures from her friends in Alberta. She has delayed and perhaps sabotaged the All-News Network plan. The others, however, which in some cases add very little to the Canadian character of the system, she said nothing about. As one of her colleagues stated four years ago: "But, Sir, you had an option". The Minister did not exercise her option.
You did not want a French-language service.

What is less well understood is that 73 cents of the increase will go straight to the cable company, in this case, Rogers. Even if there had been no new specialty services added to the basic service, Rogers would have received a 60cent per month increase.
Canadians who are watching this debate on cable may be interested in knowing how their cable fees are set. The cable industry is the only territorial monopoly in Canada whose profits are unregulated. The industry is certainly regulated in general terms, but it is still a special case in terms of profits. What is the result of this situation? As Andrew Roman of the Public Interest Advocacy Centre rightly notes:
As a result of this regulatory vacuum, Canadian households pay far more than they should for cable television services. The proprietors of cable licences have been given what has been called "a licence to print money" and, when they wish to get out of the business, to sell their share at a price at which they earn a profit on the sale of the printing press itself.
Cable prices are regulated somewhat by the CRTC. The rates are set by the commission on the basis of a number of variables. The Caplan-Sauvageau report listed those as "the quality of service provided by the operator, additional service proposed, the difference between the projected rate and the rates charged by other operators in the region, the intent of the operator to share the cost involved in providing the service, and financial need." It should be noted that the economic profile of the cable industry prepared for the Caplan-Sauvageau task force by Moss, Roberts and Associates noted the "lack of any formalized, explicit policy for rate setting."
As the Public Interest Advocacy Centre pointed out in practice, "The main criterion is how much other cable companies charge in the same area". The centre also stated: "It... means that the greediest or least efficient cable operator will apply first for a rate increase and the others will follow shortly to preserve consistency in the area whether they need the higher rates or not. Over time, the rates tend to reflect the needs of the least efficient system, which provides
September 20, 1988

service to a majority of customers to earn very handsome returns indeed. In effect these small systems are used by the larger ones as an excuse to overcharge the majority of Canadian subscribers". Think about that, Madam Speaker, to overcharge the majority of Canadian subscribers.
We in the NDP believe that cable companies deserve to earn a fair rate of return. However, Canadian consumers will pay approximately $1 billion for cable services this year, and they deserve to know that they are not being overcharged for those services. Cable, like the local telephone company, has a monopoly. One cannot change companies. Consumers deserve fairness. The amendment that we have proposed goes a fair distance to ensuring for Canadians just that fairness.
It should be noted that the cable industry is, on the whole, enormously profitable. This is particularly true in large metropolitan areas, although some small companies are less profitable. It was Canadian cable subscribers who, in large part, underwrote Ted Rogers' billion dollar American empire from the money that he made in Canada.
If one looks at the financial projections for cable over the next 15 years, as assessed by the broadcasting task force, one can see how profitable it is. If it is assumed that cable fees rise with the rate of inflation, the average return on equity would be some 25.7 per cent. This is almost double the rate of return on equity that Bell Canada is permitted, which is also a carrier and regulated.
We can well inflate the figures for the biggest cable companies. As stated earlier, the result is that consumers are and will be paying far too much to the cable monopolies. The proper criterion is NEED. Andrew Roman has stated: "The correct criterion for determining need is to allow the shareholders a return on their investments of similar risk.
This amendment picks up some of the language regulating Bell Canada in the Railway Act. We believe that it will provide the appropriate basis for setting cable rates in the future, in order that the consumer, as well as cable shareholders, are protected. It is a significant amendment for average Canadians who have cable and have to pay cable fees.

Madam Speaker, first I want to thank the Minister for indicating that she is prepared to accept Motion No. 63 and an amended Motion No. 66. I understand and appreciate the nature of the amendment. The Minister is perfectly right that we make that move and we will do so in due course.
Speaking to Motion 54A, moved by my friend from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), I think what he is asking makes good, solid sense. He is saying the CRTC already does this so why not put it into law?
The determination of rates outside of the cost of living adjustment I do not happen to agree with. In this case I think it should be part and parcel of the rate hearing. If there is one
Broadcasting Act
thing I have had more complaints about in the last three months, this is it. I am sure the Minister has had the same thing in her riding, although perhaps my riding is somewhat different as it has a very large English and French division. Some of the decisions of the CRTC now being implemented, on the French side by Videotron which has the responsibility to implement them, and on the English side by CF Cable, which has the option to implement them, have created some very serious concerns for both anglophone and francophone viewers in my riding. The cost increases in particular for programs which they do not want have created a lot of concern. We have even had a city council pass a motion expressing its disappointment and concern over the cost and content of the carriage in the system that they are hearing about from their constituents. Therefore, I certainly will support Motion No. 54A because I think it would perhaps settle some of the problems.
The Minister has addressed the panel and its obligation to consult. The Minister has not addressed the last one in this series, the deletion under Motion No. 64. This was brought to our attention by the Agency for TeleEducation in Canada. They felt very strongly that "another area which gives us cause is the cabinet authority in Clause 25(1 )(d). This new power appears to allow the Governor in Council to prescribe the terms under which licences can be issued to otherwise ineligible groups". Perhaps the Minister would care to respond to that. If she is refusing to allow that amendment, it would be only fair to advise the people concerned why she finds it not in the interests of the Canadian broadcasting system and where it might interfere with provincial jurisdiction.
I went to outside legal counsel and they suggest that Cabinet could direct the CRTC to prescribe conditions for provincial educational broadcasters. It strikes them that specific directions on educational programming issues challenge provincial jurisdiction over education. This appears inappropriate unless we are to reach new agreements through federal-provincial communications meetings or appeal to the courts.
The Ontario Ministry of Culture and Communications took the view that the power in Clause 25(1 )(d) was too detailed and could lead to interference with the CRTC's normal regulatory and licensing process. The Minister must make a decision and let the community up there know why she is either rejecting or accepting this power which is seen as prescribing conditions for the issuance of licences to provinces. It is seen by others as diluting the federal powers in broadcasting as outlined in 3(h)(3) which I addressed in Motion No. 22.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to put to the House a proposition concerning Motion No. 66. I cannot move this because I seconded the motion, but I understand there is a disposition by other Members to do so. What we are trying to do here, with the Minister's concurrence, of course, is to remove the obligation under Clause 25(2) for the Minister to consult. She would then accept, 1 think, the amendment of the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) which says that the Minister

shall consult with the commission before the Governor in Council makes an order in subsection (1). We are removing the "s" from "subsections" and removing the "and 2". 1 understand another Member of this House is ready to move that amendment and I just wanted to explain that what we are doing is removing the consultation obligation in Clause 25(2).

Madam Speaker, before I move the appropriate amendment I want to add my comments to those of my colleague from Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who suggested in Motion No. 54A that we add immediately after line 34 at page 11 the following:
"(a) determine whether the rates charged by distribution undertakings are at all times just and reasonable, and if they are not, may revise them accordingly."
We all know that the CRTC regulates cable companies and to a certain extent the fees they charge. It is appropriate, when you consider the role cable has come to play in the lives of ordinary Canadians, that we be somewhat more vigilant in determining what they charge to individual subscribers. I know in my constituency that people who have the opportunity to watch the proceedings of this House do so only if they are hooked up to a cable system. If for no other reason, we ought to be more sensitive to the role cable companies play in influencing the awareness of issues by Canadians.
Consider for a moment that cable companies have a monopoly in providing a community service, yet to a certain extent they are unregulated when it comes to the fees they charge. I know that as a Member of Parliament I have received correspondence on a number of occasions from people who feel that certain cable companies have been charging excessively for the services they provide. We have all heard that, at least in certain instances, owning a cable company or being a major shareholder in a cable company is akin to being able to print your own money. It is extremely lucrative. I would emphasize that is true in certain cases. I would not want to suggest that every cable company is a major money-maker because I am aware of some that are not, and which for a variety of reasons have got into some financial difficulty.
However, this very reasoned amendment from my colleague is simply saying that the rates charged to subscribers be just, reasonable and fair. I do not suppose anyone would suggest that rates charged should be anything other than that. We all recognize that as only appropriate. If rates became excessive for whatever reason, this motion would enable an intervention and revision of those rates.
I think we all recognize that at times having an outside organization keeping an eye on the goings on of a cable company with respect to their fees would be appropriate. I know the Minister feels this way herself because of the issue raised by my friend regarding the All-News network. All of us who have been supporters of the CBC over the years recognize the quality service that it has provided and the role it has played in the development of the Canadian ethic. I think the proposal for an All News network was a good one.
You didn't want a French-language one.

Yet the Government, I hate to say in its wisdom because I do not think it was wisdom, because of political pressure decided not to approve the license and enable the All News network to proceed, much to the disappointment and chagrin of all progressive Canadians. Setting that aside, I think this motion put forward by my colleague is again a motion that is simply asking us to be just and reasonable. I cannot imagine anybody not supporting this.
To go on to the point made by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) regarding a small change to Motion No. 66, which I understand now has the approval of all Parties involved and makes a good deal of sense, I would like to take this occasion to move an amendment to Motion No. 66. I move:
That the motion be amended in the last line by deleting the words:
"and 2", and removing the "s" from "subsections".

Madam Speaker, I think it is very important for those who have not completely read the Bill to take a good look at it with regard to Motion No. 54A. I want to point out that Clause 3.(1)(r) states:
Distribution undertakings ... provide efficient delivery of programming at affordable rates ...
Then Clause 5.(1) requires the commission to implement the policy found in Section 3.(1). Clause 5.(2) requires the broadcasting system to be regulated in a manner that facilitates the provision of broadcasting to Canadians. Furthermore, Clause 9.(1 )(b) permits the commission to impose conditions of license to implement the policy in Clause 3.(1). Clause 10.(l)(k) allows it to make regulations to do the same thing. In other words, Madam Speaker, this issue has been addressed in the Bill. Obviously we understand the reason and the necessity for affordable rates of television throughout the country.
One other comment I would like to make is with regard to Motion No. 64. The question was raised by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone) whether or not this applied beyond the scope of municipal cable companies. This clause was put into the Bill in the first place to rectify a problem that was raised by the Standing Joint Committee on Regulatory Instruments which found that the 1968 Bill did not meet this requirement. It applies solely to municipal cable companies in a way that they exist, say, in isolated communities on the Prairies or in any province. It has nothing whatsoever to do with educational broadcasters, which are independent of the province and have to come to the CRTC for their license.

Madam
Speaker, there being an amendment, that allows me to speak again. I think it is a very specious argument that there are affordable rates buried in the Bill in these clauses.
September 20, 1988
It is right up front in the major section.

I think you have to look at them very closely and put that together. I do not think for a moment the Bill tackles the problem of excessive cable fees. If you double my phone bill, for example, you could still call it an affordable rate and I could still pay it. But the phone company is regulated as such. It looks at the rate of return-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You get some value.

-what kind of rate of return it is getting here compared to other businesses, the service that is provided, et cetera. This amendment attempts to deal with the real issue. It talks about the rates, making sure at all times that they are just and reasonable and they can be revised accordingly. This really sets it down. I do not know what the cable companies have on this Government or this Government has with the cable companies. They seem to be kissing cousins. They are more than kissing cousins in this one.
In this Bill the cable companies are the big winners. They get to broadcast as well as just transmit. As I said before, it will make it really difficult to regulate their rate of return in the future because of that. If the Minister would just listen, what is it that these cable companies have with the Government? They are immensely profitable. I cited all the reports. Canadians are complaining. We have complaints about the increases. Why is the Government not tackling that? Why will it not meet the demands of the ordinary Canadian here and not accept a clause like this which gives the CRTC some real power, some real terms, not just previous terms that were in the Bill, and some real criteria with which to regulate those rates so that average Canadians and their families can pay a fair rate of return for their cable, which is an essential service.
Let me conclude by saying something to the people in British Columbia who will be watching this at a time three hours earlier than where we are here. Many people in B.C. think that provincial politics are the really important politics and that federal politics are just out there and not that important. I say to them, and I hope they will consider this, that their telephone rates are regulated federally, cable rates could be regulated partly federally, and their income taxes are regulated federally and so on. So many of the day-to-day issues are regulated by the federal Government. British Columbians should take interest in the upcoming federal election and look at what Party is prepared to deal with fairness for average Canadians and their families. This is the perfect issue here with cable rates. This Government is very cozy with its big, rich friends in the industry, ignoring the interests of average Canadians. This is why it is rejecting this amendment today. Make no mistake about it, Madam Speaker.

Madam Speaker, I was listening to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I think his amendment put forward here is an appropriate one. It states:
Broadcasting Act
That Clause 9 be amended by adding immediately after line 34:
Determine whether the rates charged by distribution, undertakings are at all times just and reasonable and if they are not, may revise them accordingly."
I cannot get together in the Nickel Belt area with a couple of people and start a cable company because Northern Cable Services has the monopoly. It has been given the license to provide the cable services in the Nickel Belt area which is made up of the City of Sudbury and a large rural community.
We are told that the CRTC regulates the cable companies. One of the things not effectively regulated by the CRTC is the question of the rates. People in the Nickel Belt area know that, for example, Bell Canada, which has been given a charter to provide telephone service in the Province of Ontario, when it wants a rate increase has to go before the CRTC to justify it. The CRTC looked at the profitability, at all the funny little games that Bell Canada used to play in the past with its subsidiaries. Northern Telecom used to charge Bell Telephone an arm and a leg for the little piece of telephone equipment that was required, so Bell Canada was always showing that it was not making money when it fact it was its subsidiaries that were doing this. After a long process, Bell Canada had to justify this. Oftentimes, the CRTC would not approve the increases. In fact in some cases, Bell Canada was forced to reduce its rates retroactively.
The same is not so with the cable companies. The CRTC has no power to determine whether in fact requested rate increases are fair, justifiable and reasonable. This amendment attempts to deal with that. It attempts to provide the CRTC with the ability to see whether those rates are fair and reasonable. I think that is what the consumers want.
Many of the consumers of cable services in my riding are retired folk, older Canadians, and television has become a very big part of their lives in retirement. We can almost call it an essential service for that element of society, yet they are captive to the rates being charged.
I think the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has put forward a very thoughtful amendment, and 1 would urge Hon. Members to support it. I think it is essential, in a regulated monopoly, that the regulating body have the power to determine whether the rates charged are reasonable and fair, not just in comparison with what other cable companies in the region are charging. That ought not to be the main factor in determining the rates. It ought to be the profitability of the company, what is fair and what the market in the local area will bear.
I have not seen any of these cable companies going out of business. The Hon. Member referred to the relationship between the Tories and the cable companies. I would like to know about the election contributions of the cable companies to the Conservative Party. I wish the Minister would show as

much spunk with respect to the CRTC and the cable companies as she showed when she interviewed on the all-news channel. I would like to see some spunk here as well.
I ask Hon. Members to support this amendment. It is fair and reasonable and I think it should be supported.

Mr. Speaker, despite the denials of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), the truth about his plans to cut further the number of his employees is emerging. A top official says that senior staff were told last Friday to put off cuts for the time being but were not told of changes to the policy of cutting 361 jobs over the next two years.
The Public Service Alliance has a document prepared by Environment Canada setting out a timetable for cutting 742 jobs over the next five years. Since Friday last the Director of Personnel Policies in Environment Canada has been muzzled after confirming the proposed cuts.
All of this is familiar. Be it toxic chemicals in the St. Clair River, PCBs, or departmental budget figures, when the story told by Environment Canada staff conflicts with that of the Minister we see desperate denials and muzzling of staff.

September 20, 1988
We hope Mr. Marks, Director of Personnel Policies, will not end up herding muskox in Ellesmere Island National Park as a reward for speaking the truth.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday, the great family of sports fans in Quebec lost a friend, a giant of the sporting world and one of its most distinguished ambassadors, Jacques Beauchamp.
Jacques Beauchamp was a man loved and respected by all, for his simplicity, his honesty, his frankness, his big heart and his devotion. The Abitibi-Temiscamingue region will keep a cherished memory of this man who did not hesitate to put his trust in one of our local people, Ghislain Luneau, also a sports journalist, who died in a tragic car accident.
Jacques Beauchamp came to our region several times and in his daily column, he regularly kept his readers informed of the people and the sports events in our area.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my fellow citizens and on my own behalf, I would like to extend my sincerest condolences to his wife and family as well as his co-workers.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government, under the pen of Erik Nielsen and the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), produced a document known as the "Buffalo Jump of the 1980s". Similar to the Liberal White Paper of Jean Chretien of the early 1970s, it proposed assimilation of Canada's aboriginal people and extinguishment of their rights.
The implementation of this plan is now in full flight. Bands presently require over 10,000 homes. These are desperately required by families presently sharing accommodations or living in substandard dwellings.
Earlier this month the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) admitted to me:
Following discussions with Treasury Board, CMHC made slight cuts this
year in its social housing program.
Over the past decade 4,295 units lapsed from CMHC programs due to poor management by the Minister and his Department, a figure not disputed by the Minister. The same
Minister has identified needs for 21,000 new units but has yet even to approach Treasury Board with a submission.
Without adequate housing or jobs there is little choice for most first citizens but to move. This, of course, is precisely what the Conservatives planned and anticipate. By adding to this, cuts in administrative budgets, economic development, and education, and refusing to settle comprehensive and specific claims, the Conservative plans for assimilation and extinguishment gain momentum.

maintopic: OLYMPIC GAMES-STATUS OF UKRAINE AND THREE BALTIC STATES
OLYMPIC GAMES-STATUS OF UKRAINE AND THREE BALTIC STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, close to 100 Ukrainian athletes are participating in the Olympic Games being held in Seoul, Korea. They are the pride of their homeland, yet none of them will be carrying the flag of Ukraine. Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were once members of the Olympic movement. Yet they, too, have been denied independent participation by Moscow.
The Soviet Government claims that these countries cannot participate independently because it would violate the Olympic Charter. Yet the President of the IOC has contradicted this claim and the Charter itself states that any nation or dependency which forms its own national Olympic committee may join.
We share in the pride of our own Canadian olympians and this only serves to underscore the injustice to the fine young athletes who have been denied, by Moscow, the opportunity to represent their homeland.
I call on the Government of Canada to issue a formal protest to Soviet officials against this flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter and fundamental human rights, and to demand that Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Ukraine take their rightful place with the Olympic family.

Mr. Speaker, I have some very serious concerns that the Government has a hidden agenda with respect to the Cape Breton Development Corporation. I believe that the Government intends to privatize this Crown corporation.
Legislation has been passed to drop the Industrial Development Division from the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Second, the Government is supporting a new coal mine in
September 20, 1988

Pictou County which will impact negatively, both on the future and the present operations of the Cape Breton Development Corporation.
There is a clear lack of progress with regard to the Lingan Mine in New Waterford. This lack of progress at Lingan Mine will cause 100 workers to be dropped from the payroll by April 1, 1989. I realize that senior members of the United Mine Workers of America are trying to consummate an agreement with the Cape Breton Development Corporation to ensure that this does not take place.
The real problem with the Cape Breton Development Corporation is here in Ottawa with the Conservative policies that relate to coal development in eastern Nova Scotia.
In addition, no effort has been exerted by the Government with regard to the Donkin Coal Mine. Here we have a coal mine ready to go into production but the Conservative Government of Canada provides monies to a new company to open a new coal mine in Pictou County.
I find this appalling in view of the tremendous history of commitment been made by previous Governments to the miners of Cape Breton.

maintopic: AIDS DISEASE-PROPOSED FREE HYPODERMIC NEEDLES FOR DRUG ADDICTS
AIDS DISEASE-PROPOSED FREE HYPODERMIC NEEDLES FOR DRUG ADDICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Ottawa-Carleton Health Department has joined Toronto and Montreal in considering giving free hypodermic needles to drug addicts to help combat the spread of AIDS. I find this type of initiative disgusting. We should be finding ways of curtailing drug use, not looking for ways to continue it.
Consider this. No diabetics receive free hypodermic needles to inject insulin each day in order to live. Diabetics did not choose to contract the disease. Drug addicts, on the other hands, chose to use drugs and they have the option to curtail their use. Diabetics have no such options. They have to inject insulin for the rest of their lives.
If any free needles are to be given, it should be to those who medically need them. In fact, these three boards of health should concentrate on helping individuals who truly require assistance rather than indirectly condoning drug use.

Mr. Speaker, today is the United Nations International Day of Peace. In calling the attention of the House to this particular day I have a couple of points which I would like to make.
First, with respect to a lot of the optimism which surrounded the INF agreement and what one might almost call a dangerously relaxed view of the world now toward the issue of nuclear disarmament, we need to remember that the INF was only a beginning and that the Canadian Government and others should be very careful that it not simply become the end of one era and the beginning of a new era of modernization of nuclear weapons through sea-launched and air-launched Cruise missiles, et cetera. It is very important that that be seen.
Second, when we talk about peace we should be careful that we do not commit the sin of the false prophets who cry "peace, peace" when there is no peace.
We should remember always those people whose oppression sometimes dwells in obscurity. I think of the Kurds of Iraq, the people who were recently massacred in Burundi, and the people of East Timor who have been oppressed by the Indonesian majority. These people do not make the headlines but are nonetheless human beings and part of our common humanity. We should be paying more attention to them when we talk about peace. There can be no peace without justice.

Mr. Speaker, Albertans are pleased to learn that Nellie Mildred Carlson of Edmonton is a 1988 Persons Award recipient, one of only five across Canada.
The Persons Award recognizes outstanding contributions toward improving the status of women in Canada by celebrating the efforts of five well-known Alberta women pioneers; Emily Murphy, Louise McKinney, Nellie McClung, Irene Parlley, and Henrietta Muir Edwards. These Five outstanding pioneer Alberta women were instrumental in petitioning constitutional amendments in 1929 to allow women to be appointed to the Senate.
Nellie Carlson has been a dedicated promoter of native women's rights in Alberta. Albertans are justly proud of the historical contributions Alberta women have made to Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, 57 per cent of Quebecers questioned on free trade believe that it will be beneficial. The Government of Quebec has made its position on free trade official and its manifesto analyzing free trade from the Quebec point of view comes out in favour of free trade.
The Leader of the Opposition in Quebec, Jacques Parizeau, has made the Parti Quebecois's position official in a preface to Bernard Landry's book Commerce sans frontieres ("Trade Without Boundaries"). subtopic: PRESERVATION OF RAILWAY STATIONS-SENATE DELAY IN PASSAGE OF BILL
PRESERVATION OF RAILWAY STATIONS-SENATE DELAY IN PASSAGE OF BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CPR still haunts the Canadian people through its former president who is now a Liberal Senator.
Bill C-205 is a Private Members' Bill proposed by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) which would help Canada keep part of its heritage by allowing us to preserve our historic railway stations. We had all-Party agreement in the House of Commons and the House of Commons committee, but preserving our heritage does not seem to matter much in the infernal other place. They have stalled Bill C-205 by having it sent to a committee for study.
The former CPR president, now a Liberal hack in the Senate, is telling this country that, after all the people of Canada have done to support and build the CPR and CNR for a hundred years, with land grants, cash grants, loans and tax breaks, it is just not important to them to preserve the physical reminders of our railroad history. This is the thanks we get as taxpayers from the CNR and CPR for ensuring their viability.
This insulting arrogance on the part of railroads continues. The latest example is the unconscionable behaviour of the Government and the CNR in the treatment of employees and independent truckers by Route Canada. It is a swindle of the taxpayers, the employees, and the contracted independent truckers.
It is with great sadness that I must report to you and the Canadian people that both the Tories and the Liberals, as well as the railroads, today stand convicted of arrogance and callous insensitivity to the needs, hopes, and history of our country.
* *
*

subtopic: GATINEAU PARK-THREATENED BAN ON DOWNHILL SKIING
GATINEAU PARK-THREATENED BAN ON DOWNHILL SKIING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was disturbed to read in the Ottawa Citizen today that consultants are suggesting that the National Capital Commission ban downhill skiing at Camp Fortune in the Gatineau Hills.
This apparently is one of the dozens of suggestions in four plans for the redevelopment of Gatineau Park over the next
five years.
I consider myself to be an environmentalist. I have spoken many times in this place on environmental issues. I strongly support greater conservation measures at all national parks, but we must strike a reasonable balance between conservation and recreation.
One of the many wonderful features of life in the nation's capital is easy access to excellent recreational and skiing facilities. To ban skiing at Camp Fortune totally, allegedly in the name of conservation, would be sheer idiocy.
September 20, 1988

Mr. Speaker, "Monsieur Jacques", as Pierre Peladeau called him so well, has passed away. Jacques Beauchamp, whom I had the pleasure to know, was a builder, a communicator, a man loved by all sports fans.
As kind and generous a man as could be, he made his mark on hundreds of journalists whom he helped and inspired and on Quebecers, man and women alike. He was a father to so many people in the trade that I cannot name them in the time available to us.
A hard worker, he was a great inspiration to all around him in journalism. An innovator, he helped set up the widely read newspaper Le Journal de Montreal.
To his family, I extend my sincerest condolences and those of my Party. To all his friends, and especially to Pierre Peladeau and Maurice T. Custeau, I want to say that I share their sorrow.

subtopic: EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT'S ADOPTION OF FUR LABELLING RESOLUTION
EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT'S ADOPTION OF FUR LABELLING RESOLUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this year Parliament successfully came to the defence of our trappers and our fur industry over the British fur labelling issue. However, we must not become complacent.
Goaded by a combination of animal rights activists and former British Labour Party MP's such as Barbara Castle and Clinton Davis, the European Parliament has adopted an antiCanadian fur labelling resolution.
The Government of Canada must redouble its efforts to protect the livelihood of Canadian trappers.

Mr. Speaker, postal rates are going up again but some residents who pay those same rates do not get equal service. I rise on behalf of the residents of Port Moody, Port Coquitlam, and Coquitlam, British Columbia, who have written to me protesting the installation of supermailboxes in their community.
Oral Questions
Mr. John Collins writes: "We are both senior citizens and I am in a wheelchair. No consideration or thought went into allotting our postal superbox. Our's is the second row from the top and hard for me to reach from my wheelchair".
Beth Christianson writes: "Collecting mail from a superbox is a hardship not only for seniors and the disabled, but also for mothers at home with very young children".
Are these mothers or fathers, as the case may be, supposed to hire a babysitter every time they have to pick up their mail?
Let us get rid of these Mulroney superboxes and give our seniors, our handicapped, and the Canadian public in general the door-to-door service of mail they deserve and have paid for.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: ROUTE CANADA CLOSURE-EFFECT ON TRUCKERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Because the Government appears to be in such obscene haste to privatize everything that moves, the Conservative Government is directly responsible for crushing and destroying the livelihood of thousands of employees of Route Canada.
Over 2,000 men and women with families to support have no severance pay, no pension benefits, and now no jobs. Three hundred truckers are out of pocket an average of $13,000 each. Thanks to the Government's policy of privatization, and the privatization of the trucking arm of CN, a couple of people now have real estate worth tens of millions of dollars, and thousands of people are out on the street and out of work.
Why has the Government, which is responsible for this privatization, not already arranged for some interim support for the employees who are out of a job as a result of this privatization, and for the 300 truckers who now have no contract, are carrying their machines under debt and are in an impossible position? Why has the Government not given some interim help until they can get back on their feet?

subsubtopic: ROUTE CANADA CLOSURE-EFFECT ON TRUCKERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on several occasions, the Minister of Labour, the Minister responsible for financial institutions and myself have explained in the House that in 1986, because Canadian National was losing $70 million, it could either shut down Route Canada or sell it-which it did-to the private sector, which meant that 2,700 workers, less the 600 for which it would become responsible later on, were able to keep their jobs. Mr. Speaker, there were two options. One was to shut down the company, while the other was, basically, to sell to the private sector and thus guarantee these workers a job. That is

September 20, 1988
Oral Questions
what CN did, and, Mr. Speaker, until further notice, if the Leader of the Opposition can show us the papers, fine! However, we have yet to see any notice of bankruptcy or other paper that would lead us to believe that the company has not only stopped operating but has gone bankrupt. If the Leader of the Opposition has such evidence, perhaps he will be so kind as to send us a copy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport is not responsible for privatization.
Every day of unemployment worsens the situation for these truckers. They need an operating licence and immediate assistance to compensate for the losses they have incurred.
When drought wiped out the harvest of Western farmers, the Canadian Government quite rightly offered several million dollars in assistance. speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
