speechtext:
that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to
September 20, 1988
amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very proud, on behalf of the Government, to rise and speak at third reading of Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act. This Bill will enable the Government to implement a major element of the national strategy on child care. As all will agree, it represents a milestone in the history of social policy in Canada and establishes child care as a separate and significant human service.
We have made child care an important social priority for the Government because we know it has become a pressing problem for an increasing number of Canadian families. Over the last decade we have seen significantly larger numbers of women participating in the workforce, and we have seen substantial changes in the structure of the Canadian family with more single parent families and two-earner families than ever before.
These factors have created a very high demand for child care services that meet the standards parents require for the care of their children. Helping to meet this demand is an important national mission. No one disagrees with the need to provide quality care for our children, just as there is no one who will deny that the availability of child care services is critical if we are to improve economic and social opportunities for women in Canadian society.
The question then is how best to provide those essential services. This has been the subject of much debate across the country. Even the special parliamentary committee chaired by the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), now the Minister of State for Transport, which was established to examine the issue and which held public hearings in 1986, was unable to reach a consensus on the best approach. The Government concluded that we must adopt a strategy that was flexible enough to support the diversity inherent in Canadian society and, above all, to be supportive of parents' rights to choose the type of care their children will receive.
The national strategy on child care represents a major step forward in the development and improvement of child care services for Canadian children. Unlike other proposals that have been raised and discussed over the past few years and which continue to be repeated today, the national strategy on child care meets this important social need in a manner that respects the rights of parents to make their own choices regarding the best means to care for their children. We must all respect that right because it is a fundamental part of our family based society.
At the same time, our strategy respects the jurisdiction of the provincial and territorial Governments when it comes to child care services. The federal Government should not, and this Government will not, dictate to the provinces the design and delivery of services that are so clearly within their own jurisdictions. Dictating to the provinces would not only be inappropriate given the jurisdictional circumstances, it would
September 20, 1988

also be counter-productive and would not meet our goal of developing a caring and workable policy.
Provinces already have a variety of child care services and programs. These services have developed over the past number of years in response to the needs of the residents of each province and in accordance with particular regional circumstances. I am pleased to be able on say that our national strategy on child care is flexible enough to build upon the system that currently exists and to adapt to the differing needs of the provinces and the families within those provinces.
Members will recall that the national strategy on child care, which I announced last December, consists of three interrelated elements: enhanced tax assistance to families with young children, a new child care initiatives fund, and a new federal-provincial cost sharing program. The first two elements of the program are already in place. The third is represented in legislation being debated for the third time today. In addition, in July I announced an additional $60 million for accredited on-reserve Indian day care services, and I am pleased with the response from Indian leadership on that issue as well.
The tax component will be of benefit to well over one million Canadian families. For parents with receipted child care expenses the maximum child care expense deduction has been raised from $2,000 to $4,000 per child for children six years old and under and for children with special needs, making child care significantly more affordable for many Canadian families.
For parents who choose to remain at home to care for their children or do not have receipted child care expenses, we have provided a supplement to the current child tax credit. The effect of this supplement will be to raise the total child tax credit to approximately $760 per year effective 1989.
The second component of the the national strategy on child care is the $100 million special initiatives fund. It will play a vital role in our goal to improve the quality and diversity of child care services across Canada. The purpose of the initiatives fund is to provide financial support to demonstration projects and applied research initiatives which meet the child care needs of special groups in society and stimulate the development of child care facilities in underserviced and remote areas of Canada.
For example, some of the priority areas which need examination include meeting the special needs of disabled children, children whose parents work part-time or in shifts during which normal child care services are not available, children from minority cultural backgrounds, and children in rural communities. Those are only some identifiable areas.
This fund has been made available since the beginning of April of this year, and the Department is already receiving and reviewing applications and awarding funding to applicants from across Canada.
The new $60 million initiative for day care for Indians on reserves will be used, among other things, to determine child
Canada Child Care Act
care requirements for on-reserve Indians, to develop and train day care workers, and to build and operate accredited day care facilities for Indian communities. Indian communities and groups from across Canada have already shown a vital interest in child care and the potential which these funds represent. By the new year I plan to announce the details of the program so that I may enter into agreements with Indian communities immediately, namely, that funds will be available on April 1, 1989.
I will now turn to the issues of debate of the last number of days, those being the key provisions of the Canada Child Care Act and the manner in which they relate to our objectives to increase the availability, affordability, accessability, and quality of child care services across Canada.
As Members of the House will know, at report stage I addressed a number of issues which were raised within the legislative committee. I would also like to take this opportunity to focus on some of the more major issues including that of establishing national standards within the framework of the Canada Child Care Act.
Passage of Bill C-144 will authorize the federal Government to enter into agreements with provincial and territorial Governments to share in the costs of the provision of child care services. The Bill will authorize the federal Government to commit some $4 billion as its share of the program over the next seven years. When the national strategy on child care was announced last December, we estimated that meeting the goal of an additional 200,000 new subsidized spaces would require a federal commitment of some $3 billion.
However, on the basis of plans submitted by provincial Governments over the last six months, it became clear that extra financial assistance would be required if we were to achieve the growth in spaces we wanted as well as ensure that the quality of the system as a whole, including existing spaces, salaries, and subsidies, continue to improve.
That is why we announced in July that the Government was committing a further $1 billion for seven years to the program. We are not prepared to sacrifice quality for quantity. Both are equally important to parents whose children will be utilizing the child care system.
During the seven-year period, what we are calling the boost period, we intend to support the creation of 200,000 additional subsidized child care spaces. In effect, this will more than double the size of the current subsidized system in Canada.
To assist provinces to meet that national goal, we will provide 75 per cent of their capital costs involved in the development of new spaces in not for profit child care agencies for the seven-year boost period, as well as 50 per cent of ongoing operating costs for non-profit and commercial agencies funded by the provincial Government.

September 20, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
We made this decision to permit federal cost sharing of provincial support for commercial agencies under the terms of the legislation because we recognize that we cannot afford to ignore the basic fact that 40 per cent of Canada's child care spaces presently are in the commercial sector. As I said earlier, the reason our national strategy on child care is a workable policy is that it works upon the system that currently exists and adapts to the regional diversity of our country.
This legislation will also permit the Government to enhance the effective rate of federal cost sharing for certain provinces through a top up provision. We have included this provision to assist parents and children who reside in provinces which are attempting to catch up to other parts of Canada in what they spend on child care.
This is the national strategy. We believe that child care facilities and services should become more equally available in all regions of the country.
Beyond year seven, the top up will continue. In addition, there will be a provision which will allow, over time, for the reduction of differences among provinces with respect to federal per child contributions.
Let me emphasize the point that what this legislation proposes is to reimburse the provinces for the costs they incur for these purposes. They must spend the money on their child care systems to be eligible for the federal funds. There cannot be a diversion despite the fact that Members opposite have said that could be the case. We are not handing over money to the provinces to spend as they see fit on services, other than those spelled out in this Bill.
Clause 4 of the legislation sets out the various terms and conditions that will form part of the negotiated agreement between the federal Government and each province. They will include the annual federal commitment to each province, the number of spaces to be created during the seven-year period, and the basis for subsequent cost sharing arrangements with respect to child care services.
Clause 4 also requires provincial authorities to specify the standards established for child care services within the provinces, the methods of enforcing these standards, and the means by which both standards and enforcement procedures will be publicized within each jurisdiction. Provincial Governments will also be required to provide evidence of the fact that they are enforcing their standards.
The standards that we are asking provinces to develop and enforce will include: child-staff ratios; the qualifications of child care staff; group sizes, both by age and by type of care; health and safety measures; and the nature of parental involvement. Some provinces will already have all or some of these standards in place. For those that do not, there will be a negotiated time period for them to put them in place.
Under the terms of these federal-provincial agreements the federal Government will not be enforcing a rigid set of national
program delivery standards across the country. The agreements may in fact result in such standards if all provincial Governments were to agree on a common set of standards. However, I am personally unconvinced that national standards are the right way to proceed. Apart from being an unprecedented direct intrusion in an area of provincial jurisdiction, rigid national standards do not meet our goal of flexibility, nor are they responsive to community values and needs that vary considerably from one end of the country to the other.
We believe that parents, caregivers, and community and professional groups are the best judges of the standards which are important to their communities and their children. They are surely in the best position to work with provincial authorities to develop and ensure the enforcement of the standards appropriate to their circumstances. This is one reason we are asking the provinces to publicize their standards so that parents can participate in the quality control of the care given to their children.
The federal Government has provided leadership in specifying areas where standards are required and in ensuring that they will be publicized and enforced. The responsibility then rests with the provinces to proclaim those standards. After all, in this matter the provincial Governments are directly accountable to the residents of each province even more so than the federal Government, due to the jurisdictional requirements within our country.
Provinces remain free to negotiate an agreement with the federal Government under the terms of this legislation or to continue to cost share child care expenditures under the terms of the Canada Assistance Plan. CAP, however, only provides operating funding. It does not provide capital assistance. Further, CAP provides only limited funding to the commercial sector, thereby excluding many of the spaces that provinces are subsidizing in commercial child care centres.
On balance, the Canada Child Care Act provides provincial Governments with significantly greater benefits over both the short term and the long term. When a province has signed an agreement with the federal Government, it will no longer be able to access the Canada Assistance Plan for the support of its child care system. Once all provinces have signed agreements, under the terms of this Act the Canada Assistance Plan will be amended to exclude references to day care. The Canada Child Care Act over the longer term is intended to replace the day care provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan. Many have said that they wanted to move from a welfare based system to a service based system. Those who vote against this Bill are voting in favour of retaining welfare for the purposes of child care.
While there are a number of features common to those two programs, the Canada Child Care Act holds significant advantages for the provinces, advantages that many provinces viewed as important and necessary to enable them to continue their efforts to expand child care. For example, according to Clause 3(2) of the Bill, provinces can negotiate and sign
September 20, 1988

agreements at any time. If, however, provinces sign prior to April 1, 1990, that agreement may be retroactive to April 1, 1988.
As I said, we have designed this program to be as flexible as possible and to accommodate all provincial requirements consistent with meeting our objectives. Where possible, we have continued to offer improved flexibility to provinces. For example, provinces made representation to us that they could not always control the pace at which new spaces would be created since in most instances the spaces would not be created by the province but by individuals or by groups. Therefore we have introduced a new provision into the agreements which will help provinces with their funding requirements by allowing for some carryover of unused federal funds from one year to the next.
I am pleased that Members opposite approved that plan. On the one hand, they argued about flexibility and no jurisdictional encroachment into the provincial area, while on other areas they seemed quite pleased to do just that.
The federal Government has made a major commitment to provisions of child care services in co-operation with the provinces. The seven-year program represents a federal expenditure of approximately $4 billion to add 200,000 new subsidized spaces, doubling and maintaining the current supply while supporting and expanding parental choices. That does not include the financial commitment of the provinces or expenditures following the seven-year period to finance child care services at their new expanded level. That ongoing commitment will provide approximately $800 million per year to the provinces to maintain their expanded systems. If we compare that $800 million to our current investment federal per year of about $106 million, it is a fivefold increase.
The strategy is a significant step forward and one within the capacity of all levels of government to afford. In fact, I think all Members of the House owe my colleagues, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), a vote of thanks in this regard. Under their direction our Government has managed the economy well. We have gained the financial flexibility necessary to embark on this major new social programming.
We now have before us this Bill which represents an historic milestone in Canadian history. It is a product of broad consultation with interest groups and citizens across the country, through not only the recent legislative committee but other forums as well such as the special parliamentary committee. It involves support to the formal day care sector and to parents using informal child care arrangements. It involves support to the family. It extends flexibility to the provinces and territories so they can develop a system best suited to their situation. It addresses the issues of availability, affordability, and quality.
Canada Child Care Act
The Bill also offers special attention and recognition to the needs of lower income families, as well as families of different linguistic and cultural backgrounds. Providing for the needs of their children is the most important priority of all parents in this country. Providing choice to parents, improving the quality of child care, and increasing the number of quality subsidized spaces available to parents is what this caring policy is all about. It is a flexible policy that is fair to all regions. It meets the needs of parents and children across our country.
I would like to thank Members of the House who worked through the past few weeks to complete the review of the child care legislation. Some have worked at it for years. I believe their efforts and deliberations have helped to shape the over-all effectiveness and understanding of this new child care legislation.
Thank you for your time and patience, Mr. Speaker. I would ask all Members not only to approve Bill C-144 in the next number of hours but also to celebrate the obvious success that it will be.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, in Canada the day-care concept is nothing new. Formerly, working parents sought help from relatives or neighbours while wealthy families would hire nurses, governesses and tutors.
The first day-care centres appeared 135 years ago in Montreal and Toronto as a result of the industrial revolution.
During World War II the federal Government, which needed women in the labour force, entered into cost-sharing agreements with provinces that were willing to set up day-care centres. At the end of the war, the cost-sharing agreement and the day-care centres thus financed disappeared, and many women returned to their homes.
Since then, a number of studies have pointed out the need for setting up a better day-care system. Since 1970, when we had the Royal Commission of Inquiry on the Status of Women, it was no longer acceptable to refuse to provide daycare, in the hope of discouraging women from seeking employment. However, the Government's present policy fails to reflect the double role played by most parents and most mothers with pre-school children who work outside the home and on whom our economy depends today.
Although fiscal measures were introduced to alleviate the burden on parents, there has never been a national program to promote the creation of day-care services. In 1986, when 52 per cent of Canadian women with children under the age of 3 were working outside the home and nearly two million children under 13 needed full-time or part-time day-care, there were fewer than 172,000 spaces in quality day-care.
The Government's hesitation cannot be attributed to a reluctance to set a precedent in the area of federal-provincial agreements, since social programs initiated by the federal

September 20, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Government are nothing new, Mr. Speaker. In the past, programs of this kind have been introduced to respond to other social needs, and more specifically, established programs financing in the areas of post-secondary education, universal health care, old age security, spouse's allowance and unemployment insurance.
Canadians have long accepted the principle of paying the cost of training and developing new generations. The first step was creating our education system. Today, most Canadians believe that a national day-care program, properly planned, is a logical extension of universal public education that would lend itself well to a federal-provincial agreement. Nor can we say that the reluctance of the present Government to show some initiative in this respect is due to a lack of information on programs that exist elsewhere.
The Scandinavian countries, Germany, France and Italy all have publicly-financed programs for pre-school children, more specifically, children between the ages of 3 and 6. In France, for instance, day-care centres were established at the beginning of the nineteenth century for the children of factory workers. In 1975, more than 30 per cent of children are outside the home and two-thirds of these are in day-care that is financed, licensed and supervised.
Furthermore, children between the ages of 3 and 6 have practically universal access to day-care. In France, 95 per cent of these children have access to a network of day-care centres and public nursery schools.
It has also been recognized that quality day-care is especially worthwhile for children from low and middle-income families. Six studies carried out over a long period in the United States revealed striking differences among children raised in poor families, depending on whether or not they had access to quality pre-school programs. Among those who did, a much higher percentage finished high school, college, professional training, while the number of teenage pregnancies dropped. They were also more likely to find jobs. They were less likely to live on welfare and the crime rate was lower.
Mr. Speaker, in addition to promoting earlier reading, the program made it possible to detect and treat far more quickly all kinds of problems and disabilities. These programs enhance the child's development without the pressure of school marks which comes into play as soon as the child enters primary school.
In the case of disabled children, the day-care system may be particularly useful for learning social skills, including tolerance and awareness of others.
The Prime Minister says he wants to set up a program to help young people shake off their drug habit, but I think if we set up a program for pre-school children and do it properly, we would have an excellent drug prevention system right there. I have said this many times. However, Canada has no comprehensive policy in this respect. In fact, in 1970 the lack of quality day-care was said to have reached crisis proportions
when the Royal Commission of Inquiry on the Status of Women prepared its report. Fifteen years later, more than
7,000	parent groups and 200 organizations that came to make presentations before Katie Cooke's group showed that lack of day-care is a recurrent source of problems for many Canadian families.
Today, the federal Government helps day-care in Canada in two ways: by granting a deduction for day-care costs and by administering a federal-provincial cost-sharing program, the CAP. This assistance for low-income families is provided on a cost-sharing basis under the CAP, but less than 20 per cent of the children below the age of six who meet the criteria have actually received a full or partial allowance. Furthermore, the contribution made by parents who raise their children full-time is not sufficiently recognized by society.
Add to this the fact that measures intended to help parents raise their children, such as family allowance, income tax deduction for children and the child tax credit, have all been revised downward and de-indexed by the present Government, to the extent that all families, even those receiving welfare, will be worse off after 1995.
Funding for day-care seems rather meager when we look at what it costs to raise children today. To the Liberals it is clear that we urgently need a genuine national childcare program. To achieve this, we must have a policy that reflects current trends, Mr. Speaker. When we look at what those trends are, we see how the Canadian family has evolved and how it is structured, the rapid increase in the number of mothers working outside the home, the regular decline in jobs in traditional manufacturing sectors where the jobs were previously held by men, and the regular increase in underpaid employment in the services sector where the majority of workers have customarily been women.
Canadians are increasingly in favour of universal day-care whose cost would be shared by the Government, the private sector and parents. The public favours various types of daycare, including home day-care, school day-care, day-care in the work place and stop-over centres. There also seems to a broad consensus on a number of initiatives that would be politically feasible, such as providing more time for family life. There have been discussions about the need for providing more parental leave under the Unemployment Insurance Act and to make more frequent use of flexible hours, job-sharing and extended leave or sabbaticals to enable one family member to spend more time with the family. All this has yet to gain recognition.
There must also be a choice, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the location of day-care centres and their facilities. I think it is extremely important to offer a choice of locations and facilities in order to meet the needs of each family. The main criteria are quality of service, parent participation and providing a choice of day-care, depending on the kind of care involved. The needs of infants, pre-school children and children between the ages of 6 and 12 are not all the same. We also have to offer a
September 20, 1988

choice of schedules. We know that parents who work outside the home and who work evenings and at night must have access to flexible hours or weekend schedules. When setting up a network of day-care services, we must consider these needs which vary from one community to the next.
We also have to set up the infrastructures. Although there is general agreement on the need to provide a universal, affordable and top quality day care system, there is no consensus on the way to achieve this. The major problem relates to the shortage of quality spaces, yet we cannot set up the infrastructure of a national program unless we promote the rapid growth of first quality and affordable facilities. Quality must be guaranteed. Mr. Speaker, practically all people agree that if we want quality we have to increase staff salaries and improve the training and qualifications of those who are made responsible for our children. Standards also have to be similar from one province to the next. And we should discuss the issue and give financial assistance. We know that most observers agree that top priority should be given to low income or single parent families. Employers ought to be given incentives to provide child care facilities at work. But with all that. . .
What has the Government done? It has produced legislation limiting subsidies, legislation limiting growth, and legislation without national guidelines. Interestingly enough, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), pointed out on Friday that even in the preamble of the legislation there is a contradiction. There the Government, thanks to an amendment put forth by the Liberals, undertook to create at least 200,000 spaces. Later, however, it says that it will make payment not exceeding $4 billion. Thus the very preamble of the Bill is confusing.
What if 200,000 spaces cost more than $4 billion? Before we even explore how the spaces are to be created, we do not know how many spaces the Government intends to create. Mr. Speaker, 200,000 spaces are not enough. The House had heard many Members this last week speak on the necessity of child care. It should now be known by all Members that one in five children in Canada is poor, and that 50 per cent of children aged six through thirteen years old are left alone after school. We have the figures showing that 1.8 million children in Canada have parents who work or study for more than 20 hours per week. That 1.8 million is the core need group.
There are approximately 200,000 spaces in Canada. The Government intends to create another 200,000 spaces over seven years. Therefore by 1995, should the Government manage to create its 200,000 spaces, 70 per cent of the children in Canada who need child care spaces will be left without them; and we call this a national strategy.
During the last weeks we also heard about the importance of adequate care in early child development. I will not go into elaborating on the head start program again. However, I will
Canada Child Care Act
point out an interesting fact that emerged recently from an American study. Committee members were all told two weeks ago that the best indicator for the successful completion of Grade 12 was not the neighbourhood, the socio-economic background, or any other factor but the child's mark in the first grade.
Before we applaud the Government for meeting a paltry 15 per cent of the child care needs over a seven-year period, let us at least recognize the social investment child care provides. Let us recognize that caring for our children before Grade 1, permitting our children to enter Grade 1 and successfully completing it, gives those children phenomenally better chances to perform as fully productive members of society. Imagine the social costs saved by society, not only in lower crime rates, lower rates of toxic abuse, and teenage pregnancy. It will also lower the rate of failed academic or professional carriers and increase the productivity of our workforce.
It is also important to note that while the Conservative Government now proposes to recognize Canada's multicultur-alism in the preamble pursuant to an amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), the Minister found himself unable even to mention the Charter of Rights and Freedoms or the Multiculturalism Act in the preamble. That is interesting, is it not? Is the Government hoping that a mention will quell the anxiety of our multicultural community by protecting them in the preamble without protecting them legally in the body of the Act? There definitely were witnesses before the committee who did not feel protected.
Then there is the issue of standards or objectives. There has been a lot of talk about federal and provincial jurisdiction, about the inability to mention standards in the Bill, and about Meech Lake. The Opposition, along with every child care advocacy association across this country, has had enormous trouble with the lack of standards set out in the Act. My colleague from Vancouver East pointed out that this might even be the first great failure of Meech Lake.
The Liberal Party strongly believes in a national child care strategy, which is why we support the idea of national standards. These would be established with the provinces and specialists in the field in order that all interested parties have a say and agree once the standards are defined. They will then be included in the legislation in order to ensure that Canadian children from Newfoundland to Vancouver, from southern Ontario to the Northwest Territories, are assured of adequate day care. Provincial child care agencies with no previously high standards would not be hampered or prejudiced in any way because they would be meeting these standards.
The Government is using $2.3 billion, it says, to encourage development of child care through the tax system. The child care expense deduction is regressive, benefiting the wealthiest taxpayer more than the middle class. Not only is this measure

September 20, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
regressive, but it assumes that all parents who must pay for child care can produce receipts which will qualify them for a deduction. In fact, the majority of parents use informal care arrangements such as babysitters, from which receipts are generally unavailable. Informal caregivers are often reluctant to issue receipts for their services because they would then have to declare all their child care income for tax purposes. Thus, the families benefiting from this provision are the wealthiest with the highest taxable income and the ability to pay for formal, licensed care.
For parents who take care of their children at home, the Conservatives propose to increase the child tax credit. This credit is refundable and, unlike the child care expense deduction, it benefits all taxpayers equally. However, the miniscule amounts of money involved would hardly compensate a mother for income while she stayed at home to care for her children. Instead of enriching the tax break for parents, giving every family a few dollars which will hardly make a dent in their child care costs, the Conservatives should have invested the entire S6.4 billion, at the very least, in the construction and renovation of new spaces, improvement of existing centres, and upgrading of salaries for child care workers.
The Liberal Party will effectively place all of its child care funds into the creation of child care spaces. There will be no resort to regressive fiscal measures. The federal Government claims that the infusion of funds over a seven-year period is a boost to the child care structure. Once such a structure is in place, after the seventh year it will continue to fund the child care system but only according to a minimum formula which will be not less than "the contribution payable to the province in respect of the year ending March 31, 1995, less a reduction in respect of the cost of capital assets, the difference being adjusted for the national rate of general inflation as determined by the Minister of Finance, with a top up fund for lesser developed provinces".
It seems to me the Government is failing completely to acknowledge the fact that we need a child care structure in this country. It deems a seven-year boost period to be enough. It deems the creation of 200,000 spaces to be enough. As I said, that meets only 15 per cent of the need. That means after the seven-year period, after the Government has finished its boost, 1.4 million children will not have places in child care spaces. There will be no program in place to encourage the creation of new places. I think the Government has to own up to the fact that this is not a national child care strategy. It is a feeble attempt to quell the demand for child care. The timing, after all, is interesting.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised to introduce a national program in the 1984 election campaign. Four years later, on the eve of an election, his Government comes up with what it calls a national child care strategy. It then, upon meeting with the provinces that in turn feel gypped by the program, adds another $1 billion to the strategy. This, however, is only to meet the need of creating the original
200,000	spaces the Government promised in its original strategy. I have spoken to the Ministers responsible for child care in many of the provinces. Ontario has had to cut back its proposed expansion by 12,000 spaces.

Mr. Speaker, the problem with these additional funds is that they left people with the impression that the Government was again adding new money while in fact it had to provide these funds to launch the program it had already unveiled in December. This was a false impression and we must set the record straight: the money recently provided by the Government was simply the money required to begin the program which had already been announced.
Nor are the provinces altogether satisfied. Quebec does not know what to expect, what with all its places in the school system. We happen to know there are now 30,000 places for school children throughout the Province of Quebec. It is made quite clear in clause 2 of the Bill under consideration that all services relating wholly or substantially to education will be cut off.
So the current program is woefully inadequate and most of our children aged 6 to 14 are still left without any supervision, without any of the services they so badly need.
The Liberal Party will develop twice the number of spaces the Conservatives promise. What about native Canadians, Mr. Speaker? We heard representatives from the Assembly of First Nations and the Inuit Women's Association, both of whom eloquently pointed out that their children were also in need of child care services. The AFN is in no way comforted by the fact that the Government has put aside $60 million for on-reserve child care because it deems that its children should have their rights entrenched in legislation and not left to the discretionary whims of the Governor in Council.
The Inuit population, not specifically mentioned in the legislation, will probably not be covered by it because it does not have on-reserve communities. It will, of course, fall under a cost sharing agreement should a province sign one, but nothing is there to guarantee that once a province signs such an agreement a culturally sensitive child care program will be provided to the Inuit populations.
When amendments were introduced at committee to modify the legislation to meet the needs of our native peoples, they were "deemed beyond the scope of the Act". It is a sorry state, Mr. Speaker, when a Bill is structured such that certain needs are so fully excluded that they cannot even be placed on the table for discussion.
Let us look at the scope of the Bill. It does not include mention of parental leave, for example. However, every committee dealing with issues pertaining to child care suggested that UIC parental leave should be increased from 15
September 20, 1988

weeks to 26 weeks. The Liberal Party would address this issue and place it within the scope of child care legislation where it belongs. The scope of the Bill might have included different types of child care settings. However, amendments were proposed to encourage child care in the workplace and child care in an after-school setting, but they were defeated by a Government that purports to encourage choices.
Perhaps the Government fails to see the link between child care in the workplace and choices. The Government will have to answer to the parents working in fishing canneries on one coast, of this country and lumber mills on the other coast, as well as to all clerks and business persons in every city of the nation. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that a Liberal Government will offer a tax write-off in excess of 100 per cent to employers creating an employer subsidized child care service.
Two of my amendments were adopted at committee, two which I hold particularly dear. One according priority to low to modest income children and one according special protection to the French or English minority of a province and to its multi-ethnic communities. On the first and foremost point, low to modest income children, we must mention the Canada Assistance Plan, CAP, which has been used to reimburse provinces which provide child care services to children of low-income families. Though CAP failed to meet the child care needs of this country, by its very nature it accorded special assistance to the neediest children first. Prior to our amendment, now Clause 4(b) of the Bill, Bill C-144 failed even to mention the needs of low to modest income children. It was this original abomination which caused witnesses from across Canada as well as the Liberal Party to plead for the maintenance of CAP in conjunction with the new legislation. This would ensure that the needs of the poorest of our children would continue to be met systematically.
I will tell you why this is important, Mr. Speaker. First, only
200,000	spaces will be created leaving very, very heavy needs unmet. As was pointed out by a witness for Ontario in the committee hearings before the Senate, the limited funds being accorded to meet child care needs will leave the provinces with hard choices to make, including choices of the types of child care to provide, the cost of user fees and, in effect, the income bracket to be served. This is unacceptable in so far as it will cause children from rich families to be in competition with children from poor families. It is essential that CAP be maintained. If the $4 billion the Government intends to pour into its alleged child care program is new money, then there should be no problem in at least maintaining CAP at its present level.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, the child care legislation is completely inadequate. I can only hope that the Government now takes heed of what the witnesses have clearly stated and reconsiders the action to be taken.
The Liberal Party policy on child care recognizing that there is a greater need will create at least 400,000 spaces over
Canada Child care Act
the next seven years. It will, after discussion with the provinces, reach a consensus with them to establish minimum standards. It will encourage the development of child care in the school setting. It will encourage the development of employer subsidized child care through a tax write-off in excess of 100 per cent cost. A Liberal Government will meet the needs of Canadian children. It will be a priority.

Mr. Speaker, I think that this day care legislation falls far short. Under a Liberal Government we would indeed make it a priority, and one of our immediate objectives would certainly be to create child care spaces at the workplace as well as establish after school day care facilities for our children.
Again I urge the Government to reconsider this totally inadequate Bill which we are debating today.

subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 66, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi)-Housing-Situation in Toronto/Surplus federal lands; the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby)-Public Service-Wages of Halifax naval dockyard workers; the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Red way)-National Parole Board-Violent offenders-Retention in prison.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp (Provencher) that Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, during World War II when women were needed to man the factories and maintain the economy in Canada, Governments recognized that child care was an essential service. So we had government funding for free day care nurseries near many workplaces. However, after the War women's work was no longer considered to be essential and subsequently child care was not a government priority. For the past more than 20 years now since the royal commission on the status of women, women have been saying that licensed day care is a basic

September 20, 1988
Canada Child care Act
requirement for women to achieve equality. It must be developed as an essential community service.
During the past 20 years society has changed dramatically. Over 60 per cent of mothers of young children are now in the workplace, either part time or full time. This trend will be maintained and indeed will increase in the future. Most mothers work because they have to. Their incomes are essential to maintaining their families, and particularly to help pay the high costs of housing.
The great increase in single parent families usually headed by females has significance for planning policies for child care. Increasing numbers of women with young children are left alone to raise children on their own, usually with very low incomes. We know that about 61 per cent of children of these mothers are poor.
It continues to be an absolutely deplorable fact that one in six Canadian children are being raised in poverty. Their mothers need child care as do average parents. Certainly teenage mothers, who have been on the increase, do as well. They need child care if they are to work, to study, or to train for the future so they will have an alternative to life on welfare.
Families have changed over the past 20 years. Relatives are not as available as they used to be to provide babysitting on short notice. Grandmothers often live far away or they themselves are working.
As my colleague who spoke previously said, we were very moved by the presentations of First Nations groups and also Inuit women about the needs of children in their communities. For native families, their children are their future. They want to be able to control and develop their own child care programs, programs that are relevant to their traditions and their communities. However, they must have adequate direct funding for this, funding that is guaranteed. As my colleague said, that funding is not guaranteed under this Bill.
Mothers or fathers who remain at home to care for children full time also need part-time child care services. This is not just for working parents. They need it for relief, for occasional recreation, for parent support programs, and for training. Many also want their children to develop socially and to be better prepared to enter kindergarten so they want half-day pre-school programs which are also child care programs.
Study after study under first Liberal and then Conservative regimes has documented again and again the need for a comprehensive system of quality, affordable services. These studies have also documented the crisis we are facing with children because of the neglect and inaction of provincial and federal Governments.
There is ample evidence of inadequate standards for child care and of the high fees which must be charged because there is not adequate funding for child care services. There is ample
evidence of the long waiting lists of children who need child care and of the inadequate training that is provided for caregivers because of the lack of capital or operating grants that exists in most regions of Canada. Child care is in a very critical situation and it has become worse in the four years of delay by this Conservative Government.
What is happening to our kids as a result of this neglect? The parents of close to two million children are working either part time or full time or are studying, yet only about 240,000 licensed day care spaces exist to accommodate them. Most of these children are cared for in very risky, informal kinds of babysitting arrangements. Fees are usually unaffordable, close to $4,000 or $5,000 a year for one child, so that average families, particularly those with more than one child, certainly cannot afford the child care that is available now.
As our committee travelled across Canada, we heard repeatedly of parents who could not get their children into day care so they often had to use babysitters they did not know or who probably had no training or they had to use family day care homes that were unlicensed. We heard of children in informal care arrangements who were entertained all day by sitting in front of television sets and of some who were neglected or abused. Parents told us they worried all day at work and often missed work when these child care arrangements broke down.
There is a high incidence of school-age children who go home to empty homes. Latchkey children form another group of kids being neglected in every province of Canada, perhaps with the exception of Quebec which has quite a comprehensive program for school age children. However, this program will probably not be covered under this Bill. This was also of great concern to the people to whom we talked across Canada and to the witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee.
Witnesses, studies, and parents have told us over and over again that a comprehensive national child care program must be developed, that it must have a full range of supports for parents, And that it must have services for children under the age of 12. New Democrats believe this must start with prenatal and post-natal care and education for parents. Family allowances must be reindexed and child tax credits must be increased to help parents with the costs of rearing their children.
Parents should have the opportunity to stay home, particularly during the period of their children's infancy, this very, very critical period in a child's life. It is very regrettable that this Government has refused to introduce amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to extend and enrich parental leave for fathers as well as for mothers so that they can have this choice when their children are young.
The NDP goal is a national child care program which should assist provinces and communities to develop a comprehensive range of affordable services. Most communities, for example, need family drop-in centres for parents and kids where there are parenting classes as well as many positive
September 20, 1988

support programs available. We need Mom and Tot programs such as the ones the YM-YWCAs offer, for recreation, relief, and informal education with good child care.
We need licensed family day care homes that take up to five children of mixed age groups. There are not nearly enough licensed, good quality day care homes across Canada. We certainly need good quality, licensed day care centres that operate with flexible hours and have separate facilities and staff for infants and toddlers. There is a great lack of care given to those age groups. We need expanded out of school care and summer programs with hot meals for school age children whose parents are working.
Facilities for child care must be accessible. The Government has completely ignored this in its legislation. Child care centres must have adequate staff to accommodate disabled children and children with special needs. There must be training programs and resources for caregivers, whether they be in family day care operations or in group care.
Some communities also need head start programs which offer enriched programs for disadvantaged children to help prepare them for school. These have been very, very successful in the United States and have reduced later problems in adolescence. Indeed, they have more than paid for themselves because of the prevention they offer.
Native child programs are needed, but they must be controlled and developed by native communities with adequate funding. Rural communities need direct funding so that they can develop their own kinds of innovative arrangements. Traditional day care centres are often relevant in rural communities. Farm families need to have a say in what is important for them. Multicultural child care programs with language training are also needed, and these are surely a federal responsibility.
In 1984, women succeeded in eliciting promises from all three political leaders to make a national child care program a federal priority. This was a political issue for women then. I can tell you that it will be an even greater political issue for women and indeed for most citizens in the coming election. It is now a public issue, and I think that most voters are aware of how society has changed and how important it is to have good child care available.
Despite repeated promises of this Conservative Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) over the last four years, where he has said that he would develop accessible, quality, affordable child care, the Government has delayed over and over again, until the very last minute, until a kind of death knell of this Parliament, before it introduced the Canada Child Care Act. What kind of priority is this?
It is no priority at all.

That is true. It shows how little this Government really cares and how all it cares about are the polls and
Canada Child care Act
trying to have a token gesture for women who are not going to be fooled when they go to the polls to vote. Canadians are tired of cynical policies on the eve of federal elections.
The government child care strategy introduced some time ago the tax measures which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has put in this year's income tax. They allocated some $2.3 billion for what we considered to be very regressive tax measures, doubling the deductions for wealthier families who could afford to pay for child care for their children, ignoring poorer families who do not pay taxes, and offering a token $200 a year to mothers in the home and those who use informal care.
We felt that this $2.3 billion was not only regressive in the way that it was used but that it should have been used for the greatest priority, which is to have affordable, quality child care available in order for mothers and families to have a choice of good care for their children.
The Government also allowed only two days of debate in our legislative committee. They rushed this again and it was after introducing an extremely inadequate Bill C-144, the Canada Child Care Act. There was no time or funds to bring in representatives from the various regions of the country and the territories. I think that this was again an insult to Canadians.
Despite this rush, however, the 40 expert witnesses who appeared were unanimous in their condemnation of Bill C-144. There was not one representative or speaker who spoke in favour of this Bill. Even the Government, you would think, could have found one supporter. That is not the case, though.
It is a restrictive piece of legislation that immediately removes child care from the Canada Assistance Plan, offers capital funds for only seven years, makes no attempt to assess or meet real needs for spaces, and provides for only about
30,000	new subsidized spaces per province or territory per year. Future growth is terminated by the end of seven years. Child care will not go away at the end of seven years. This plan to allocate $4 billion for 200,000 spaces is only a start, and a very meagre start at that. Along with the present spaces it will not even meet a quarter of the needs of children across Canada. We believe that it is very short-sighted, indeed.
I would like to mention the five worst points of the Tory Child Care Act and elaborate on them. First, it offers funding for too few spaces. Second, it establishes no national objectives for the first new major social programs since medicare. Third, it entrenches the present system of poor quality and unaffordable child care services, leaving it up to provinces to determine how they will use federal child care funds rather than requiring that these funds be used to improve the quality and to develop new kinds of child care services. Fourth, it caps funding and restricts growth at the end of seven years. All indicators show that the needs for child care will have expanded from what we now have, not diminished. Poorer provinces will not have a top up at the end of seven years, and there is no way that they can continue their services without it. We also have the whole question of funding for new spaces.

September 20, 1988
Canada Child care Act
Instead of assessing the real need for child care services in Canada and developing a rational plan, phase by phase, as we have done, for gradually meeting these needs, the Government has arbitrarily chosen 200,000 new spaces as its goal and slapped this on as the subsidy for the next seven years. As I said earlier, this only doubles the amount of spaces that we have now. It is far, far from adequate.
We know that we cannot do everything during the first few years, but certainly we could do a lot more. As my Leader said in Vancouver, we would have increased this number within four years under our program while retaining the Canada Assistance Plan. It would have cost $2.3 billion. There should certainly have been a much greater increase in the number of spaces.
We have also said before that the growth rate under the Canada Assistance Plan is now 15 per cent, and under this new program it will be reduced to a 10 per cent growth in spaces. What kind of progress is that?
Our New Democrat plan would offer direct grants during the first phase of development while maintaining the Canada Assistance Plan. As I said, it would have presented 200,000 subsidized spaces at the end of four years. We would have progressively developed it from there, with adequate shared funding over the years, into the next century.
We believe that any national plan must be based on real needs and must plan for the future. We criticize this policy of the federal Government, and we wish that it had put the tax money into increasing spaces as well.
There are no national objectives, and this is the first major national social program since medicare. Medicare spells out national objectives. We have the five principles of medicare. It has been a fine program, and we are very proud of it.
Unfortunately we cannot be proud of this child care program. It should be a landmark in the development of good social policy. It has not even conformed to the requirements the Conservative Government made under its own Meech Lake Constitutional Accord, where federal spending for social programs was to be based on the national objectives. It ignores the Canada Health Act.
The Minister refused repeatedly to accept any of our amendments in committee which would have inserted objectives into the body of the Act, even his own objectives which were pretty limited. He deliberately confuses national objectives with provincial standards, which of course are under provincial jurisdiction. The federal Government has an obligation to ensure that families and children across Canada have adequate access to programs.
Just before I move to the closing of my remarks, I would like to move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word
"That" and substituting the following therefor:
That Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the
provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in
consequence thereof, be not now read a third time but be referred back to the
legislative committee for the purpose of reconsidering Clauses 3, 4, and 5."
I outlined earlier the other concerns that we have with this Act. It entrenches the present inadequate system of child care which is different in different regions. It should be encouraging provinces to improve the quality of care. Instead, it allows them to continue with untrained workers in some programs and it allows some provinces to use the money just for subsidies while not putting any into operating grants. There is no assurance at all that programs will be developed for children over five and under three, for disabled children, and for family day care homes.
The Canada Child Care Act is very restrictive in that it grandfathers the capital funding at the end of seven years. I have said how inadequate it is that this is a seven-year program. It is a seven-year fiasco. It really restricts child care programs rather than developes national child care for the future.
Finally, the Act requires provinces to give up share funding under the Canada Assistance Plan for children in need and those likely to be in need. This concerned many witnesses and it concerned us. We tried to get this amended because we do not feel that poor children are protected under this new plan. There will be great competition for very few spaces, and funds are not guaranteed for children in need who must have some priority.
Our Party, in our minority report "Caring For Canada's Children", put forward a national child care program with seven national objectives. It is a three-stage plan that is cost effective and allows the system to grow into the year 2,000 and beyond. I want to stress once again that New Democrats want a comprehensive range of child care programs so that parents will have choices to meet their special needs.
We are not advocating compulsory, institutionalized care for every child in Canada as other Parties, in particular the Government, like to claim that we are advocating. We want a practical, phased-in plan that will develop realistically with the ultimate goal of achieving child care that is accessible in all communities, that will give parents choices, and that is an essential available service, as it is in most western European countries, in the same way as education is.
I call on the Conservative Government to resist the political games it is playing in order to respond to the gender gap in the polls and to resist the token pre-election gesture it is offering in the child care field. After waiting four years it is forcing this completely inadequate program through the House after two days in committee and very few more in open debate.
This program is not going to please women voters. They know how inadequate it is and what a disappointment it is. The Prime Minister, once again, has let Canadians down on a very important promise. Surely children are more important than nuclear subs. This country has the kind of caring citizens
September 20, 1988

who put children first and will not tolerate the neglect of our children that we are experiencing under this Government.
It is time we had a comprehensive child care program which is positive, which stresses quality, which is non-profit in nature-because that is the best kind of quality care-which will have well trained workers paid good wages, and which will offer a range of services in every community: north, south, east or west; rural or urban. Let us do it right. Our children deserve the best.
I call on the Government to withdraw Bill C-144. Through this motion we have asked that it be referred back to the legislative committee for reconsideration. Better still, call an election immediately. Let us have a new Government to put forward a New Democrat child care policy.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair has heard the amendment of the Hon. Member for Vancouver East and finds it to be in order.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question. My daughter is like many young wives who have young children but also have to work in order to help meet the mortgage payments. I have, therefore, watched my two grandchildren spend a considerable time in day care centres. I have been impressed by the hard work and devotion of the people working in day care centres, but I have also been impressed with the necessity for them, in these non-profit day care centres, to work for very low wages, not much over the minimum wage in the Province of Manitoba.
I am puzzled about why the Conservative Government's proposal and the proposals of the Liberal Party, both here in Ottawa nationally and the Liberal Party in Manitoba, would permit the funding by Governments, federal and provincial, of day care centres run for a profit.
I cannot blame the operators of privately owned and operated day care centres for wanting to make a profit. After all, that is the legitimate objective of every private business. If they have to make a profit, is it not axiomatic that the wages of the people working in those privately owned and operated day care centres will have to be much lower than those working in non profit day care centres?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for a very important question. I want to join him in acknowledging the devotion of child care workers across this country. It is the most important job in Canada, I would say, yet they probably are the least recognized. In fact, one witness said that it was the poor helping the poor, poor mothers helping poor mothers very often, because their wages are so atrocious.
I would like to remind the House that in order to qualify caregivers need at least two years of post-secondary education. In many provinces, and I must mention the Province of Alberta in particular, they do not require training. They
Canada Child care Act
require only that caregivers be 18 years of age. This is not good enough from a standards point of view.
Of course, the best paid caregivers are those who are unionized, but even unionized centres do not pay high enough wages because they simply do not have sufficient money coming in from fees or subsidies to improve that.
The Member was talking about commercial day care. I agree with him completely. It is not just our own political bias about the commercialization of services for children. Objective research studies have been done, and I can think of at least three, which showed that on average the quality of child care in commercial day care centres is lower. There are some very good private centres, but by and large the only way to make a profit is to pay lower wages to the people working there and to charge higher fees to parents. But you can only go so far in that direction or you will not have any children.
In addition, caregivers tend to burn out more quickly as a result of carrying heavier work-loads and there is a higher turnover of caregivers. Children need continuity, particularly when they are away from their own parents. They need to have a loving person who is their constant and is there to give them attention every day.
One of the things that was lacking in this Bill, and we tried to get it amended, was a conversion clause. Many private operators that we heard from, particularly in the Atlantic region, are mom and pop operations that are not making a profit. In fact, they are using their own homes and probably taking a great loss. They are doing it because they love children, because there is a need, and because they need a job.
They have told us that they would be far happier if they were able to convert to non-profit child care, if there was an agency that would help them to get proper equipment, that would help them to get capital funding for a decent building, and that would help them organize a parent body. They then, rather than getting hardly any take-home pay, would have a decent, fair wage.
I think that most of the smaller operators of profit-making day care across the country would be persuaded, with proper incentives, to convert to non-profit care. They would have the advantage of training programs offered by parent organizations, of creative toys, and of enrichment programs. It is also important for those family operated day care homes to be licensed and affiliated with a non-profit agency. It is another area where the care is very sporadic and where I am sure parents who take children in the home would like to be connected with some kind of outside agency in order to provide better service and have better pay.

Mr. Speaker, I was pleased that the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) raised the policy of the Liberal Party in Manitoba because I believe it points out one of the basic differences between Liberals and New

September 20, 1988
Canada Child care Act
Democrats with respect to child care. We have a difference with the Government as well, obviously, but some Canadians might be under the impression that because we both oppose the child care Bill there are no significant differences between the Liberals and the New Democrats. We have come to see what those differences are just recently in Manitoba, for example, where the Liberal Party of Manitoba has not criticized or opposed the decision of the Conservative Government there to extend public funding to profit making day care centres. I believe that should be on the record.
We know that many Conservative back-benchers often seem to regret the way in which society has developed, and the way in which many families now have both parents in the job market. They suggest that it detracts from the traditional family situation where most often the mother was at home looking after the children.
This points out to me a problem with Conservative philosophy. Certainly one of the main reasons so many families need two incomes is to pay the mortgage. I recall when I first became interested in politics in the late 1960s and early 1970s, when the NDP called for measures to reduce land speculation to prevent the incredible inflation of housing prices that occurred then and which is occurring again, particularly in Toronto. Yet any time one would move to curb the free enterprise market that creates the economic situation in which families feel both parents and even the kids sometimes must work to pay a $435,000 mortgage that was only $135,000 five years previously, Conservatives say it cannot be done because it interferes with the market-place. Conservatives should make up their minds. What do they value, the family or the marketplace?
For the last 20 years their real priority, their idol, has been the market-place. If the market-place happens to drive families on to the streets or make it impossible for people to stay at home, then they just have to live with that. Conservatives can get up to make speeches regretting the passing of the traditional family, but do not do anything about it because they do not want to interfere with free enterprise.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague who is indeed a philosopher in his own right, has pointed out the weaknesses in both the Liberal and Tory philosophies on child care.
He is quite right that the Liberal Party in Manitoba, as well as nationally, is quite in favour of commercial child care. It has said that the funding should go to for profit child care.
The situation is the same with respect to care for the elderly. Operations that function primarily as businesses to make a profit are really not consistent with good quality care. We challenge the Liberals on that point.
The Hon. Member is quite right that the Conservatives face a real dilemma with their philosophy. On the one hand they would like to send all women back into the home, I am sure. That was the dilemma they faced in trying to come forward with a child are program. While they profess to recognize the family, it is that Party which deindexed family allowance, deindexed the child tax credit, and imposed more taxes on families than on taxpayers without children or on corporations. One must question the conflicting philosophies of the Conservatives.
