subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE MEDIA ROYAL COMMISSION ON NEWSPAPERS (1981)
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE MEDIA ROYAL COMMISSION ON NEWSPAPERS (1981)
speechtext:
That a special committee of the House be established to consider what action has been taken by the government and former governments with respect to the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Newspapers (1981), and that the committee be empowered to consider which of the recommendations should be implemented and, in particular, the recommendations made by the Commission with reference to Thomson Newspapers Limited.
He said: Mr. Speaker, since there might be those in the House who are perhaps unfamiliar with the Royal Commission on Newspapers which brought in its report on July 1, 1981, I felt I should begin my remarks by reminding Hon. Members that this was a commission on which Tom Kent was chairperson, Gordon Spears was a commissioner, as was Laurent Picard. If I could summarize it briefly, the thrust of the commission report was that it was felt that there was an undue concentration of newspapers in the country and that perhaps this resulted in a less than favourable freedom of the press. There were certain questions raised about ownership of not only newspapers as far as chains were concerned but the fact that certain instances were cited wherein chain ownerships were also linked to conglomerates.
Based on that type of analysis, the report came up with various recommendations which I hope to deal with today. Even if one does not believe in all the recommendations-and certainly I do not believe in them all-or if one believes in none of them or, in fact, if one believes only in some of them, it is important that we as legislators, and the most senior House in the country, at least consider the evidence and the information that this commission put before the country linked, if you like, Mr. Speaker, with its recommendations.
One other matter which I should perhaps clarify is that the actual report was triggered by the closing down The Winnipeg Tribune and The Ottawa Journal. In the forward to the report it is stated:
The Winnipeg Tribune and The Ottawa Journal closed their doors on August 27, 1980. This commission in direct response to that event was created six days later.
In short, it was conceded that there was a certain anxiety at the time that an already concentrated situation was perhaps becoming that much more concentrated.
In a map that the commission includes on page 10 of its report it points out that chains at that time controlled 94.6 per cent of the total circulation in British Columbia; 96.2 per cent in Alberta; 100 per cent in Saskatchewan; 87.1 per cent in Manitoba; 60.6 per cent in Ontario; 95.9 per cent in Quebec; and throughout the Maritimes it was generally the same,
Newspapers
although Nova Scotia was just 26.6 per cent controlled by chains. I think that a compelling case is made in the report which demonstrates the concentration that existed as far as chains in the daily newspaper field were concerned.
What I mainly want to deal with today is what happened after the report. Were any of the recommendations implemented? To the best of my knowledge, none were implemented. I will come back to one instance wherein there was temporary implementation of one, only to be withdrawn later. Also, was there ever any further study given to the questions that were raised in the report?
First, I would like to touch on what some of these recommendations were all about. On page 237 the commission had this comment to make:
The ownership and control of most newspapers is today highly concentrated under interests whose business concerns extend far beyond the particular newspaper. Much of our press, consequently, is not itself dedicated exclusively to the purposes of the press, to the discharge of its public responsibility. Extraneous interests, operating internally, are the chains that today limit the freedom of the press.
The chain you will note, Mr. Speaker, that is referred to there is the chain in a binding sense. That is what the commission stated is limiting the freedom of the press.
In answer, then, what can be done about it? It suggests, for example, that there is room for a Canada newspaper Act and that it would provide for a resistance at least to a further concentration of newspaper power in the country.
Many of the recommendations, and I should be frank about this, I feel contemplate the possibility at least of undue government intervention. The commission tried to be very guarded in its comments that that was not its intention. Anything that we say today I think we should weigh in the context that I am certainly not speaking for direct government intervention. I am speaking in the context of asking this. Is there not something worth considering in what the royal commission reported on back in 1981 and, specifically, what has happened?
The only instance that I know of anything coming out of this study was a directive which was given to the CRTC by the Government of the day asking that it refrain from granting TV licences or radio licences in communities where the applicant was, for example, the local daily newspaper. I do not know whether that directive was ever acted upon by the CRTC. It was subsequently withdrawn. To the best of my knowledge there has been no direct implementation of these recommendations.
Let me first deal with the suggestion of the Canada newspaper Act. The report states that while the local monopoly of a newspaper is a problem in itself, often reflected in profit maximization by an impoverishment of editorial comment, the worst feature of concentration is not the ownership of several newspapers by one company, it is their ownership by a conglomerate, a company having or associated with extensive

September 20, 1988
Newspapers
other interests. As an example of this type of conglomerate Thomson Newspapers is cited.
I think most Elon. Members are familiar with the Thomson empire. For those who are not, I recommend that they take a look at the 1988 summer issue of The Financial Post wherein the trees of various conglomerates of Canada are shown. Under the title: "Ken Thomson-Read all about him" the various concerns that Lord Thomson controls are listed. Of course that includes Thomson Newspapers which is 61 per cent owned by a private company owned by the Thomsons; 74 per cent of Hudson's Bay; 100 per cent of The Bay, 100 per cent of Simpsons; 100 per cent of Zeller's; and 100 per cent of a real estate company called Markborough Properties. On the international Thomson organization side there are various other interests such as oil and gas and book publishing and that type of thing.
I would simply like to summarize the Thomson situation as one in which when the royal commission looked at the situation it found that Thomson had 40 newspapers in Canada. That is the same number that it has today. I am referring to daily newspapers here. The Globe and Mail is of course one of the newspapers that it has. Its growth since the 1981 report has been mainly in the United States. When I speak of growth, it is truly sensational.
The Thomson organization-and when I refer to these figures I am referring to Thomson Newspapers Limited-are running at roughly a 40 per cent pre-tax profit margin on revenues. In smaller communities it is even higher than that. The net result is that in 1987, on earnings of $1.95 billion it was able to have a net pre-tax income of $379 million. Royal Securities, RBC Dominion Securities, has indicated that it believes that profit will get up to over $.5 billion by 1990.
Let us make one thing clear. There is nothing wrong with a business concern making a profit. The bottom line is what insures the solvency and the continual prosperity of that organization. What we have to ask ourselves is whether the tremendous concentration that Thomson is showing in a business sense of developing what it calls "cash cows" is in the best interests of a free responsible press in this country.
The formula is very simple. If one maximizes revenue and minimizes costs, the net result is editorial staffs are shortchanged as far as remuneration is concerned. As a result of the underpaying of many of the personnel, it is very difficult for those papers in the Thomson chain to get the type of seasoned, well-educated employee that one would normally expect to handle what is one of the crucial jobs in any democracy, and that is the reporting of the news.
I am not talking about so-called interpretive reporting. I would suggest that what we need, as much as anything in this country, are responsible journalists reporting what actually is the news, and hopefully conveying it through their newspapers to their reader who can judge accordingly as to what action he
or she should take on whatever topic may be relevant at the time.
I would like to touch very briefly on some of the recommendations that the commission has come up with in the context of what it feels is an over concentration. It points out there should be a divestiture of either the The Globe and Mail with Thomson retaining the other 40 newspapers that it owns, or it should retain the The Globe and Mail and sell off the other 40 newspapers. We know that has not occurred. What indeed has happened, and if you are interested, Mr. Speaker, I could give the specific profits, is that those Canadian newspapers have generated an income that, in 1980, the year that the royal commission was looking at, had Canadian revenue of $284 million. By the end of December, 1987, that had gone up to an even $.5 billion. That is a nice increase during the 1980s. As far as the income is concerned it is even more dramatic. One finds that the segmented operating income in Canada has jumped from $62 million to $157 million, as far as Thomson Newspapers is concerned.
Where was that money used? Was it used to ensure that there was a high calibre reporting staff, that the editorial content that appears in what is generally called the news hall of a newspaper was of a high calibre? No. It was substantially used to give the cash flow needed to make further acquisitions in the United States. That is where the growth has been; in short, the funelling off of those profits out of the Canadian newspaper empire, short-changing the production of the newspapers in this country, so that there could be further acquisitions made in the United States. Today the chain has 160 newspapers; 103 daily and 5 weekly newspapers are in the United States. The remaining are 40 daily in Canada, and 12 weekly newspapers.
The first comment I would make is that the Royal Commission I have referred to asked that Government consider the desirability of a divestiture of this empire. Is it worth revisiting to determine if that divestiture would have been wise? There is a five year time given for the divestiture, or has the inaction been the appropriate course to take?
I would then mention that there is a rather novel approach of a taxation nature to try to get more competition into the newspaper field in Canada. The recommendation had two parts. It was suggested that there may be room to give an added tax write-off to those who would like to invest in new newspapers, the concept being something similar to what one could obtain by going into the film business in Canada. For example, if somebody wanted to raise $1 million, the royal commission asked: "Would it be possible to give a tax credit so that somebody who is raising $1 million to get into the newspaper field in Canada would at least have that incentive?" Again there was a formula for the adjustment of taxes within a newspaper in accordance with how much editorial content was put into the newspaper and what the expenditure was in generating satisfactory editorial content in the newspaper. It was a surtax, and tax credit approach. Again, I would recommend that Hon. Members who may be interested in this
September 20, 1988

subject take a look at the report and see the nature of that recommendation.
Another recommendation was the role of the editor in the newspaper. They suggested that if one has this highly concentrated ownership such as Southams, The Toronto Star, or the Thomsons, perhaps there had to be something done to ensure an independence at the editorial level. The suggestion was that editors-in-chief be asked to sign a contract that would be binding on the owner to ensure that he would have certain security of tenure during his employment, and that if he had to make some tough decisions that might be embarassing to the owner or somebody else connected to the newspaper, he would not feel that his job was at stake as a result of making that decision.
The commission pointed out, and perhaps I should quote page 246 which states:
Overall, the structure is most certainly not one that can give any confidence-
That is the present industry structure:
-that newspapers in Canadian communities are edited independently of the other business interests of their chain or conglomerate proprietors. The structure is, in other words, incompatible with the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association's own declaration, in its 1977 Statement of Principles on this point.
It then quotes what the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publisher's Association stated should be the principle:
The newspaper must hold itself free of any obligation save that of fidelity to the public good ... Conflicts of interest, and the appearance of conflicts of interest, must be avoided. Outside interests that could affect, or appear to affect, the newspaper's freedom to report the news impartially should be avoided.
In short, the association pinpoints what appears to be an inherent defect in the system that the commission found.
I know my time is quickly running out. I would like to simply conclude by saying that I believe Hon. Members should revisit the Royal Commission, look at the evidence that it mustered, look at the recommendations that it proposed, and ask themselves: "Are you indeed happy with the way the freedom of the press is functioning in the country at the present time, and in particular can it be bettered?" Democracy at any time needs a truly free, objective, responsible press, and that is what I am hoping measures in future will attempt to attain.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE MEDIA ROYAL COMMISSION ON NEWSPAPERS (1981)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this debate with respect to a special committee of the House being formed to decide which of the recommendations of the Kent Commission report will be implemented by the Government.
I must say that in listening to the Hon. Member, a former champion of free enterprise and the free market system, I was a little bit puzzled about his defence of government intervention in such an important matter as concentration of ownership. I recall myself and my friend, the Hon. Member for
Newspapers
Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), advocating that the Government intervene or examine closely the excessively high profits of multinational drug companies. We also recommended that certain foreign takeovers of Canadian operations be examined in detail as they were under FIRA. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) would obviously argue the Government's side and say you have to let the free market take its course. We now find our efforts have been rewarded. We now have before us in the House a conversion. The Hon. Member now agrees with and understands fully the importance of the Government of Canada taking its public responsibility very seriously.
I found the subject matter of this motion very interesting because I do not believe the Hon. Member talked about a fundamental underpinning of that sector of our economy, namely freedom of the press. He may have alluded to it but I cannot recall him mentioning it in his remarks. That issue has to be first and foremost as we proceed down this long path. Quite frankly, there is nothing inherently wrong with what the Hon. Member is asking for. I would hope that the House would concur with this motion, although it only deals with one particular industry.
The Hon. Member took great pains to point out many things about the Thomson chain of newspapers. Perhaps as we proceed along in this debate, this particular Parliament, and even into subsequent Parliaments, we will discover the real reason why he wishes to do that. However, corporate concentration and control is not a problem just for the newspaper industry in this country. It is part and parcel of a growing problem for Canadians everywhere.
I had to be careful because I did not want to laugh while the Hon. Member was speaking, but when you have the major mergers that are taking place in this country, increasing corporate concentration in the retail sector, and then hear the former Minister say the Government now has to look at a particular sector, one has to ask, rightly so, as no doubt my friend from Nickel Belt will, why all of a sudden this concern about corporate concentration in the newspaper industry?
I do not want to take all the credit. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt will want to share the credit with me for finally convincing the Hon. Member to see the correctness of our suggestions regarding government intervention and the public interest.
I, too, would want to examine some of the recommendations contained in the Kent Commission report. However, it is important to note that there is both provincial and federal jurisdiction involved with respect to how the recommendations would be implemented. It does not necessarily follow, either, that with corporate concentration you are automatically going to see editorial writers or particular newspapers slanting their views in a particular way. I think the best example of that was the K. C. Irving case when it was alleged that K. C. Irving acquired a complete monopoly of English language newspapers in New Brunswick to complement other media and diverse

September 20, 1988
Newspapers
industrial holdings in the province by purchasing the remaining independent newspaper. The Supreme Court of Canada acquitted Irving in that case by holding that no presumption of detriment to the public arises merely from the fact of a monopoly.
However, I would want to go back, not necessarily to argue that case again, but as the Hon. Member suggested, to review some of the recommendations and some of the cases which have followed that particular case. We would re-examine whether or not that ruling of the Supreme Court at that point is really relevant in 1988 and beyond.
It should also be noted that although there was not much action subsequent to the Kent Commission, Bill C-226, the Daily Newspaper Act, sponsored by the Hon. James Fleming, formerly the Minister responsible for implementation of the Kent Commission report, received first reading in the House on March 12, 1984, as a Private Members' Bill. Under that legislation no one would be able to control newspapers with an aggregate of more than 20 per cent of all daily circulation. That provision would not have any retroactive application.
I bring that to the attention of Members who might be under the false impression that no activity whatsoever followed the recommendations of the Kent Commission. In fact, that Bill would require any non-media company acquiring or establishing a newspaper to demonstrate to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission that any such newspaper would be managed independently of the non-media company's other interests.
I repeat that an issue which the Government of Canada should be intricately involved in is the issue of corporate concentration and the effect it is having on the Canadian economy. It is absolutely essential. The Hon. Member raises the issue of the newspaper industry, but there are many other industries and sectors of our economy where we have a high degree of corporate concentration, and the Government of which he is a part has refused to take any concrete and specific action to address those important concerns.
In conclusion, I find nothing inherently wrong with the suggestion of the Hon. Member. I would hope that the conversion we have seen here today will continue beyond the imminent election and that we will go into the 1990s secure in his support for measures affecting other sectors of the economy which we deem to be important.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE MEDIA ROYAL COMMISSION ON NEWSPAPERS (1981)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this debate because I come from the riding of Duvernay and the City of Laval where we have several very important weeklies.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian publishing industry is thriving in my riding, to the extent that every week we almost have a war of weeklies. I simply cannot understand how these people manage to put out such quality papers with such limited financial resources and without any tax incentives or postal rate discounts, yet most of these weeklies are delivered right to our doors free of charge.
The newspaper publishing industry has always been the subject of particular consideration on the part of Governments because of its dual characteristic, either commercial or cultural. Given their vast land expanses and living next door to a giant, Canadians have long since acknowledged the significance of a way of expressing themselves which makes up for their regional differences and strengthens this original and diversified human fabric which is the source of unequalled pride for all of them from coast to coast.
Aware of this problem and concerned over their role in the establishment and expansion of a genuinely Canadian publishing industry, in recent years the various Governments have taken steps to help Canadian publishers, first and foremost through the publication distribution assistance program and Bill C-58. With the program to assist the distribution of publications, in January 1987, the Government announced a thorough review of the postal subsidy program for publishers, which allows eligible publishers to mail their publications to readers at preferential rates that are much lower than the commercial rates of Canada Post. This review

September 20, 1988
Newspapers
was pursuant to the recommendations of the Nielsen Task Force, in 1986, to the effect that publishers of dailies and periodicals be consulted as soon as possible in order to agree on an acceptable timetable for the phased reduction of the postal subsidy.
Reacting to economic constraints to reduce the federal deficit and wishing to maintain a strong, original publishing industry, the Government tried and succeeded in reconciling its financial objectives with the needs of Canadian publishers and readers. In April 1988, speaking to an audience mainly made up of distinguished representatives of the Canadian press, the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) announced that the postal subsidy program would be maintained at approximately the same level of funding as it then was, namely $225 million a year, for the next five years. The program will from now on be called the Publication Distribution Assistance Program, which better expresses the Government's intentions to support the press and the objectives of the program itself.
The postal subsidy program for publishers predates Confederation and is directly derived from our European cultural heritage. In 1710, the British Postal Act gave back control over postal systems in the colonies. In 1851, the British Post Office transferred to the English colonies control over their own postal services, which until then had come under the British Postmaster, and stipulated that they could set postal rates as they saw fit within their territory. By 1855, the territories that were to join the Canadian Confederation, strongly influenced by the colonial traditions advocating the circulation of information and ideas, had abolished the postal tariffs on newspapers. In 1867, an Act of the first Canadian Parliament established a Canadian postal service for citizens throughout the country.
The then Postmaster attempted to impose high postal rates on newspapers. That attempt was met with strong opposition from the industry. They asked the then Government to roll that decision back and establish free postal distribution for newspapers. Faced with that opposition, the Postmaster amended his proposal and introduced a low postal rate for newspaper distribution in Canada.
Since 1867, successive governments continued to apply that de facto policy of low rates to newspapers, and later on to other periodicals, under what is now called the second class mail or the publications distribution assistance program. Mindful of the basic goals of the program, they all wanted to ensure easy and widespread dissemination of information to every possible destination across the land, for both educational and democratic purposes. The postal program seemed the best way to meet this objective.
As the Canadian publishing industry developed, the objectives of the program changed as well, so that today, we can define the three main objectives of the policy governing it as follows:
A)	encourage communication: i.e., promote the spread of the printed word at an affordable cost everywhere in the country that Canadians live;
B)	encourage culture: i.e., promote the dissemination of printed matter from Canada in order to strengthen our cultural identity;
C)	encourage industrial development: promote the development of an ever more prosperous publishing industry in our country, in spite of keen foreign competition.
Today, 144 daily newspapers, which means practically the entire daily press in Canada, and over 600 Canadian weeklies-half the total number in Canada-benefit under the program. Generally speaking, national daily newspapers mail only a small percentage of their total circulation. However, 45 per cent of these mailings go to rural subscribers who otherwise would have trouble obtaining these papers. There are forty regional dailies that distribute more than 10 per cent of their circulation by mail, while 15 small daily newspapers depend to a large extent on the assistance they receive under this program to serve their subscribers by mail, for instance the Guardian and Patriot in Charlottetown and the Shebrooke Record in Quebec. Today, 466 local weeklies may deliver free of charge the first 2,500 copies of each issue in rural communities with a population of 10,000 or less. Without the program, these weeklies would probably be unable to survive. Other weeklies enrolled in the program pay reduced postage rates which help them continue their publishing activities.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be correct to say that the present Government has not only fought in favour of the Canadian publishing industry but has also won many battles on its behalf. Whether we are talking about the postal subsidy or Bill C-58 or free trade, the Canadian publishing industry has come out a winner. Like its predecessors, the present Government has recognized the vulnerability, the uniqueness and the importance of this sector of our economy and has agreed to make available all the necessary resources, financial or otherwise, to maintain a publishing industry that is representative of Canadian society and the communities across this country.
My concern, Mr. Speaker, is that they have so much to do and so little money to do it with, and if they could continue to have these benefits, it would enhance the quality of newspapers in our small communities.

commission was created with good reason, I think, as a result of events that took place on August 27, 1980, when, on that day, the two largest newspaper chains were involved in the closure of two major newspapers, one in Winnipeg and The Journal here in Ottawa. Where there was a joint interest of those two chains in Vancouver and Montreal, the Southam interests bought out the Thomson interests.
The commission presented a report, including a number of regulations and recommendations, directed to both Government and industry. These recommendations flowed from the commission's conclusions on the state of competition within the industry. It found that the trend to chain ownership in the newspaper industry compromised the freedom and independence of the press, Canadians' access to diverse sources of news and opinion, and press quality. It felt that action by the Government was needed to protect Canadians' political rights with regard to which the press plays a major and central role.
The commission urged that the Government strengthen the then existing competition legislation. "Break up the chains", they said, so that there would be one newspaper with one owner. Prevent cross-media ownership, that is newspapers owning radio stations. Create a publicly-owned newspaper or a chain of newspapers, something on the model of the CBC. On and on it went.
A review of the Government's response to that commission report shows that action was taken, not to the degree that some might have wished, and it might not have been as wide ranging as the recommendations of the commission itself, but with respect to the subject of cross-media ownership.
The Cabinet of the day accepted that media ownership patterns did present problems which Government should address. Direction to the CRTC was issued by the Governor in Council in July of 1982. It prohibited the granting of broadcasting licences or the renewal of such licences to applicants who were proprietors of daily newspapers and whose major circulation area substantially encompassed the same market as that of the broadcasting undertaking. Exceptions were allowed, of course.
In every case but one the CRTC renewed the licences of the applicant. In the one case, involving the New Brunswick Broadcasting Corporation, the licence was renewed on a conditional basis and for a shorter period of time. It should be noted that the New Brunswick Broadcasting Corporation took its case to the Federal Court of Appeal and successfully appealed the authoritative direction. In other cases, the direction resulted in a number of structural ownership rearrangements and arms-length standstills to create agreement within the industry.
With respect to the issues arising from the Kent Commission regarding the business operations of newspapers, the Government of the day released legislation of a draft daily newspaper Act in July, 1983. It proposed the following: To
Newspapers
limit further concentration of ownerships by barring acquisitions which would raise any individual or chain's share of national daily newspaper circulation above 20 per cent; to protect and promote editorial independence it would require non-media companies to give notice to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission of its intent to acquire a daily newspaper and to demonstrate that such acquisition was in the public interest. Further, to promote editorial quality and public accountability in the operation of the daily press, it required the establishment of a national press council independent of Government, and by offering incentives through matching grants for the establishment by Canadian newspapers of new inter-regional or international news bureaus.
The general reaction of the critics to this proposed daily newspaper Act was that even if the actual legislation was benign with regard to governmental involvement, an Act which addressed the daily press would be on the books and would make it easier to introduce substantive amendments in the future, and would lower the threshold of public concern about governmental involvement in the news media or in the freedom of the press.
In the view of the critics, the problems attributed to the highly concentrated ownership suggested that this concentration should be dealt with instead within the context of other concentration of markets. In this regard, they supported the proposal that amendments should be made in the Combines Investigation Act rather than in a single legislative common Bill.
While the proposed daily newspaper Act was never really introduced into the House, as mentioned earlier this evening, a Private Member's Bill was introduced by Mr. Fleming in May of 1984. It was based very heavily on that proposed legislation.
Responsibility for the Government's legislation was assigned to the Honourable Judy Erola. In November of 1984, an article appeared in The Globe and Mail to the effect that she felt strongly that concentration of newspaper ownerships and other issues raised by the Kent Commission should be dealt with in a revised Competitions Act.
With respect to the issue of a national press council, she is quoted as saying that the industry "was on a path that was a very healthy one" and that the "threat of the newspaper Act was basically the reason why they decided to move on press councils and doing a bit of self-government, self-policing, which was more effective than otherwise".
Since that time, this Government has introduced amendments to the then Combines Investigation Act, now the Competition Act. It is widely felt that this general law of general application is an appropriate means to address concerns of corporate concentration primarily through news mergers and abuse of dominant positions and provisions. I thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity tonight to pursue a question I asked of the Government on September 16 of this year. In fact, it is a question that I, as a Toronto Member of Parliament, have been on my feet about on a fairly regular basis. I have been trying to press the Government to do something about its responsibility in the area of housing.
It is sad to note, in the dying moments of a dying administration, that in the last four years the administration of the
September 20, 1988
Conservative Party has clearly abdicated its responsibilities in the area of housing. More and more the Government has cut back on and slashed various programs that were in place from previous administrations and has passed the political buck for housing to the municipalities and the provincial governments.
It has cut back on the social housing subsidies for non-profit and co-operative housing by $9.6 million. It cut the RRAP funding by 25 per cent. It terminated the RHOSP program which helped first time home buyers to own their first home. It cut non-profit housing in 1986 from 25,000 units to 17,500 units. Total CMHC subsidies fell by almost 20 per cent in 1984. Between 1984 and 1986 capital funding was cut by 61 per cent from $439 million to $267 million. In addition, the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program was cut by almost 51 per cent. These are only a few examples that I have the time to outline in the short time I have available to me. In these four years there has been a regression in the federal role in housing.
I take offence to the fact that on the eve of a national campaign, rather than dealing with the substance of the federal housing issue, rather than addressing the housing crisis of affordability in Metropolitan Toronto and other urban centres where there has been a housing malaise in terms of affordability, the Government has preferred to deal with cosmetic surgery and perceptions. It has announced, in the few days remaining of this Parliament, a Minister of Housing. That was somehow supposed to give the perception that the Government was interested in the housing issue. I am not sure that Canadians, particularly in the urban centres, in my own municipality of North York and in the Metro Toronto area, are going to be taken by this late conversion, if you will, on the question of housing.
That is the first part of the question that I raised on September 16 and on other days in the House of Commons with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski). The other aspect I raised was the announcement last Friday of the provision of some 50 hectares or 123 acres of Downsview air force lands for what was deemed to be affordable housing. As I mentioned in the House on a number of occasions, I was pleased that at least there was a step in the right direction in using some of the surplus lands for federal housing projects.
However, I was distressed to learn that there was no commitment on behalf of the federal Government to provide the sewer lines that are necessary to put up the kind of subdivisions they are talking about. The federal Government knew about this two months ago when it met with North York city officials. The President of CMHC, Robert Jarvis, and his chief engineers, went to North York and were told, in clear terms, that the sewer capacity was absolutely nil in that area. The feds not only put out a news release to say that they were going create this housing, but there was obviously the expectation that they would come across with a price tag of upwards of $200 million for the sewer infrastructure, both local and metro.
September 20, 1988

In addition to that, I found it amazing that they would call it affordable housing when 75 per cent of the homes would be built by private developers at existing market rates. I asked the Government to up the 25 per cent to at least 35 per cent of the entire project to meet the provincial standard and, in addition, to encourage the private developers, as the provincial government in Ontario does, to have the private housing development include 25 per cent for affordable units. Otherwise, we would only be putting up on Downsview air force lands homes that are selling in Metropolitan Toronto for an average of about $225,000 to $230,000.
In closing, I say that the Government should not only get involved in cosmetic surgery but should get involved in the substance. Let us talk about an affordable housing scheme on Downsview air force base. Let us come through with the sewer commitments that would make it a reality. Otherwise, it will only be a fairy tale project simply in time for an election call.

Mr. Speaker, may I assure the Hon. Member that the federal Government and Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation are fully aware of the Toronto housing situation and are monitoring the market very closely.
The federal Government is promoting access to the security of home ownership in a number of ways: Through the provision of public mortgage insurance, mortgage backed securities, policies to promote moderate and stable interest rates, and more generally, good economic management. Low interest rates have produced record housing starts.
In 1987, net migration to Toronto totalled 61,200. That is triple the average per year reported for the 1976 to 1982 period.
This high level of migration has significantly increased the demand for housing. This resulted in 46,518 housing starts in 1987, an all-time record. In 1988, starts are forecast to reach over 40,000. Demand has outpaced the ability of the construction industry to supply sufficient number of houses.
The federal funds that are provided under the federal-provincial social housing programs are targeted to needy households. A great deal has been accomplished in the Toronto area. The social housing portfolio is now 100,657 units of federal and provincial subsidized housing.
As mentioned in responses to previous questions, the Government spent about $250 million in social housing expenditures in the Toronto area in 1987. This figure is approximately 18 per cent of the total federal social housing budget. In 1987, the federal and provincial governments added, under the terms of the federal-provincial agreements, an additional 2,150 units.
The recent announcement by the federal Government that Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation would develop

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-WAGES OF HALIFAX NAVAL DOCKYARD WORKERS
PUBLIC SERVICE-WAGES OF HALIFAX NAVAL DOCKYARD WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address the issue of wage parity in the Public Service of Canada. On August 31, 1988, I questioned the Minister of State for the Treasury Board (Mr. Lewis) respecting the wages paid to workers in the ship repair unit at CFB Halifax.
Briefly stated, this raises the long-standing issue of wage parity between ship repair trades on the East Coast and the West Coast of Canada that requires some explanation.
First, let me describe the ship repair unit at CFB Halifax, commonly known as the dockyard. This ship repair unit provides support to Maritime Command, Canada's Navy, with repairs to the fleet and maintenance of the fleet as well as refit and repair of equipment. This means establishing the facilities, skills, trades and talents necessary to perform these functions in normal times and in times of crisis.
Let us simplify the whole matter and say that what is really required is a competent and capable workforce. Meeting that requirement necessitates adequate compensation. What we have to do is find a method for adequately compensating our workers, not only in the ship repair unit but across the Public Service.
I believe the workforce at the dockyard has every right to reasonable compensation and every right to complain that reasonable compensation is not being paid, particularly when we look at their brothers on the West Coast. We must recognize the comparability of wages in regions and across Canada. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, the workers at the dockyard are represented by the Government Dockyard Trades and Labour Council-East. I have had occasion to speak to them. I believe they fairly represent the views of the 1,800 workers in the ship repair unit.
Let me deal with the question of wage parity, with particular reference to the ship repair workers on the East and West Coasts. It is not a new problem. It goes back to the early 1970s when a distinction was first made between the wages paid to workers on the East Coast and the West Coast. I will update it to 1985 when 1 had occasion to ask the Minister to review the policies with respect to payment of wages. That is to say equal pay for work of equal value.
I received a response in 1985 from the then President of the Treasury Board who referred to a problem on pay parity between home economists and occupational therapists and wrote this to me in a letter:
-resolution of the complaint demonstrates the joint union-management approach to be a responsive vehicle to satisfactorily address issues of longstanding concern regarding equal pay for work of equal value.

September 20, 1988
Adjournment Debate
I would be the first to agree that that is an appropriate method to address these differences. It is union and management, workers' representatives and government representatives getting together to resolve this dispute. But it has not worked in this case.
In June of 1988 when I met with representatives of the Government Dockyard Trades and Labour Council to discuss this matter I undertook to address the President of the Treasury Board, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), and deal with the matter of wage parity. I received a response from the Minister shortly thereafter in July of 1988. The problem was a very specific one. The Minister indicated that in order to comply with the request for wage parity it would require over a 32 month period a wage increase of 36.1 per cent, as opposed to the offer that had been made of 11.5 per cent. One can see that it is a very substantial problem.
The Minister also pointed out, and I would like to read from the letter:
Regional differences in rates of pay do exist in the private sector and the Public Service endeavours to reflect these differences. Currently, about one-fifth of all federal public servants are paid on some form of regional pay basis.
In July of 1988 the Minister indicated that in her opinion the regional pay differences were justified. However, that requires us to look at the principles involved in pay for Public Servants.
I know that in 1977 the Government's position was very clear. It was stated in the policy paper:
The approach that the Government intends to pursue in compensating Federal public servants is one of average comparability of total compensation with a representative sample of private sector employers.
It was very clear that there were three principles involved in settling wages of public sector employees, our public servants. First, the public sector compensation must be fair to both the employee and the taxpayer. Second, the public sector compensation should be related in a reasonable and an acceptable way to the private sector. We more or less concede that government wages should trail the private sector. Third, there has to be proper collective bargaining, responsible collective bargaining to arrive at the actual dollars and cents. Nobody disputes those principles. What is in dispute is what has happened.
The dockyard council makes a very clear case that in 1975 the differences were not too great. In fact, the ship repair unit received 93.4 per cent of what was considered a comparable base wage. By 1987 it had dropped to 77 per cent of comparable wages in comparison to other areas. For example, the ship repair unit wages in comparison to municipal employees had dropped from 113 per cent to 91.29 per cent. I do not want to dazzle anybody with statistics. I simply want to say that there has been a dramatic change over this almost 10 year period. Today the East Coast workers are paid less than 85 per cent of what West Coast workers receive. That amounts to more than $3 an hour.
I am sure that everybody in the House of Commons would agree that that is not fair and that something has to be done. The hope for the future is a mediation process which the President of the Treasury Board has mentioned, and which I understand is now taking place.
My message is the following: In this mediation the proper officers have to consider the principle of wage parity. They have to move to reduce the discrepancy that has arisen over the years. The workers on the East Coast require and demand fair treatment, and they are entitled to fair treatment. On behalf of my constituents at the CFB Halifax dockyard, I ask for fairness.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ken James (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-WAGES OF HALIFAX NAVAL DOCKYARD WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak to this very important subject that has been brought to our attention by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby). He has a great interest in his constituents and the workers on the East Coast, particularly in the Halifax area. As the Hon. Member is aware, the issue of wage parity between the East and West Coast ship repair employees is at this moment the subject of mediation between the parties. In view of the fact that today it was mutually agreed that neither party would comment publicly on that dispute while this mediation effort is under way, I am not prepared to comment on the specific outstanding issues between the parties in that labour dispute, and I am sure that the Hon. Member would not wish me to do so.
Recently there has been much discussion with regard to the issue of wage parity within the Public Service, and in particular over the practice of successive governments' long-standing policy of paying regional rates of pay to certain groups of Public Service employees.
The Treasury Board as employer has traditionally attempted to negotiate regional rates for groups in which employees are located in two or more regions where outside data indicates significant variations in rates of pay among various regions in Canada, and where the mobility and the area of recruitment of the employees are limited.
There are presently approximately 43,000 unionized employees in 11 occupational groups in the federal Public Service who receive regional rates of pay. Regional rates have been in effect for some groups for many decades, and this policy has been embraced by many previous Governments.
Both the Pay Research Bureau and the Conference Board of Canada have surveyed the practice of regional rates prevailing in the private sector. Employers with operations in more than one region apply this practice in varying degrees, based upon the type of occupational groups that they employ. The practice is most prevalent for operational, administrative, and technical support positions. In its soon to be published report, the Conference Board of Canada, based on preliminary data received to date, has identified that 47 per cent of the respondents paid regional rates to their clerical and support positions.
September 20, 1988

The Hon. Member can see that this practice is quite common for many private sector employees in Canada.
It is for those reasons that the Treasury Board as employer continues to embrace the concept of paying rates of pay for certain occupational groups that are based on regional labour market conditions prevailing in the private sector.
I thank the Hon. Member for Halifax West for bringing this important point to the attention of the House of Commons.

NATIONAL PAROLE BOARD-VIOLENT OFFENDERS-RETENTION IN PRISON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where were you on July 24, 1986? Think back, carefully, Mr. Speaker. Where were you that day? Were you out on the golf course? I know that you like playing golf. Were you at the lake? I know you enjoy a little recreation. Were you in your constituency office working hard? This date was two years ago this summer, Mr. Speaker. Think very hard.
You do not have to scratch your head, Mr. Speaker, because you and I were both here in the House. We were called back for one or two days to deal, on an emergency basis, with Bill C-67. You remember that debate. The Bill was supposed to ensure that federal prisoners incarcerated in our penitentiaries who were considered violent would not automatically be released from prison after serving only two-thirds of their term, the way the previous legislation read. They could be kept in prison until the end of their term and not released on this ridiculous business called mandatory supervision.
I do not know about you, but I was rather pleased to be here at that time and take part in that debate and see that legislation passed into law. I felt the Bill was going to help restore the faith and confidence of Canadians, what perhaps might be called the silent majority of Canadians, in our criminal justice and parole systems, and in the National Parole Board itself.
Here we are two years down the road and what has happened? Did Bill C-67 do what it was supposed to do? Did it restore the confidence of Canadians in the system? Did it make sure that violent offenders were kept in prison to the end of their term rather than being released early? If it did, why is it that in Toronto earlier this year one Melvin Glenn Stanton, described by police as a dangerous sexual offender, after being convicted of bludgeoning to death a 14-year-old girl, was released to a halfway house in Toronto? He then went missing from that halfway house and, as you know, was subsequently convicted of the stabbing death of one Tempa Conter in Toronto.
If the Bill had worked the way it was supposed to work, why was it that again earlier this year in Toronto one Herbert Ray Smith, described by police as violent and mentally unstable and sexually aggressive toward women, was released on mandatory supervision? Again, he walked away from a halfway house. Why was it that earlier this year, again in
Adjournment Debate
Toronto, one Kevin Paul Mott, considered dangerous by police, was allowed out on a two-day pass and again walked away from the halfway house even though he had previously been convicted and had a record which included five robberies and assaults with dangerous weapons? If that Bill C-67 which you and I came back here to deal with had been effective, why was it that again earlier this year in Toronto one Lawrence James Munro, who was charged, convicted and imprisoned for rape and assault and was considered violent, was out in a halfway house and again walked away?
It is no wonder, with that sort of record, that Canadians continue to have anything but confidence in our criminal justice and parole systems. Recently, as you know, a poll was released which showed something like 68 per cent to 70 per cent of Canadians said they had absolutely no confidence whatsoever in the criminal justice system.
You know that this message has got across to the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), apparently, and he says he is going to do something about it. In June of this year he announced that he was going to make changes in the parole system. You will remember he said that he was going to abolish the system of earned remission. He was going to replace it with a short statutory period not to exceed 12 months. He was going to reduce the time in which prisoners were eligible for full parole from one-third to one-half their sentence, and he was going to limit day parole eligibility to six months prior to full parole eligibility. That is not going quite as far as the Sentencing Commission wanted in their recent report. They said we should abolish parole altogether. However, it would seem to be moving somewhat in the right direction.
That was announced in June. We have been sitting all summer on an emergency basis. We have not seen any Bill. We have seen nothing other than a draft Bill that was submitted to the House. The Solicitor General has gone on to say, as you know, that in granting parole the risk to the public should be the only criteria for that. In fact, when he defines that he says that parole will be granted if an offender does not present "undue risk of re-offending while on parole".
What has been happening all this time? Surely that is what has happened. We have had an undue risk of re-offending because all these people have been re-offending while on parole. Words are not enough any more. The public has had enough words and wants some action. When are we going to get some action, Mr. Parliamentary Secretary?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to respond to the penetrating analysis supplied by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway).
In the summer, 1986, as the Member has said, this Government acted to close one loophole in the process of releasing violent offenders, that being the passage of Bill C-67. As

September 20, 1988
Adjournment Debate
Members will recall, its purpose was to ensure better protection of the public from dangerous offenders by authorizing the Parole Board to keep such offenders in custody until the last hour of their court-imposed sentence if necessary, even if they had earned remission in the penitentiary.
Not only did the Government act responsibly in promoting Bill C-67, and not only is it working generally as intended, but we know that we must and we are prepared to go further as was promised at that time.
In July of this year as you have just heard, Sir, the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) announced major new proposals to reform the parole system in Canada. On August 25, these proposals were tabled in the form of draft legislation in this House.
I might go on to point out that the Parliamentary Committee on Justice and Solicitor General's Review of Sentencing and Parole has resoundingly endorsed these proposals, as has a sizeable portion of the public. Under these reforms, inmates who have committed violent crimes will be required to serve one-half of their sentences or 10 years, whichever is less, before being eligible for full parole. Currently all federal inmates are eligible after serving one-third or seven years.
This new measure has been introduced to ensure that there is more balance between sentences imposed by the court and the decisions made by the parole system. To replace mandatory supervision, the Solicitor General has proposed a short
statutory period, never to exceed 12 months, for transition to the community prior to the end of every sentence, but always subject to the detention provisions of Bill C-67.
The actions of the Government are intended both to protect the public better and to support the efforts of very dedicated and professionally responsible correctional workers trying to do their best to protect the public within the limits of the law. I believe we owe a debt of gratitude to these professionals and the community agencies for their dedication to this thankless task on our behalf. The Government is committed to ensuring better the safety of the Canadian public. The Solicitor General has acted on this commitment and continues to act on it. With the support and encouragement of all Members of the House, particularly those with the understanding of the Member for York East we can make this country a safer place for everyone.
